utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, I propose to give the decision of the Trial Chamber in relation to the Prosecution's application yesterday. The Prosecution has included in its list of the remaining witnesses which it intends to call in its case in reply or case in rebuttal, as Rule 85 calls it, one witness to whom I shall presently refer as VG117. According to the short description provided, the evidence which she is to give is that she saw the accused, Mitar Vasiljevic, at the Vuk Karadzic school in Visegrad representing himself as being associated with the Red Cross and registering a large group of people there. The circumstances in which this is alleged to have occurred, so far as is here relevant, is that these persons were thereby encouraged to believe falsely that the Red Cross would assist them to be relocated. Mr. Domazet, for the accused, has objected that this evidence is not properly in reply. A substantial issue in the case is whether the accused was present in Pionirska Street during the afternoon of the 14th of June, 1992, encouraging a group of Muslims who had been brought to Visegrad that day from Koritnik to enter a house or houses in that street by giving them a guarantee of their safety for their onward trip by bus the next morning to a Muslim centre some distance away. Some witnesses have given evidence that as part of that encouragement, the accused represented himself as being associated with the Red Cross. It is reasonably obvious that if such a representation were made by the accused, these persons would more readily have been prepared to comply with his encouragement to enter these houses because of the well-known connotation the Red Cross has for the protection of non-combatants. It is also clear that this representation forms an important part of the Prosecution case as it may assist the Prosecution to establish that the accused was aware that something untoward was to happen to those persons. Most of those persons died later that evening when the house to which they were later transferred was set on fire, but it is, of course, very much in issue as to whether the accused could be said to have had knowledge that that was to be their fate. These allegations made by the witnesses were put to the accused when interviewed by the OTP's investigator, and they were denied by him. That interview -- that interview was tendered as part of the Prosecution case in chief. None of the Prosecution witnesses who gave evidence in support of that case appears in any way to have placed reliance upon an armband said to have been worn by the accused as indicating an association with the Red Cross. The accused denied the evidence of the Prosecution witnesses when he was called as a witness in his own case. Other witnesses called in the Defence case did refer to the armband. One gave evidence that he thought that the armband did indicate an association with the Red Cross, but other Defence witnesses deny that it gave any such indication, despite prior written statements they had made to the contrary. The particular significance which the various Defence witnesses did give to the armband was not always consistent. The evidence which the Prosecution seeks to call from VG117 would, if accepted, tend to suggest that the accused had, on another occasion, represented himself as being associated with the Red Cross in order to encourage Muslims to do something which he wanted them to do. It has not been submitted that such evidence is irrelevant to the issue in question here. The objection very properly taken by Mr. Domazet is that it does not constitute evidence in reply. The Trial Chamber agrees entirely with the submission Mr. Domazet has made. The issue as to whether the accused represented himself as being associated with the Red Cross in order to add strength to his encouragement of Muslims to do something he wanted them to do arose fairly and squarely in the Prosecution's case in-chief as soon as the record of interview was tendered. It was open to the Prosecution to call VG117 in its case in-chief in relation to that issue. Her evidence could and should have been given at that time. Nothing occurred for the first time during the Defence case which gives rise to a case in reply upon that issue. In particular, the departure of the Defence witnesses from their prior written statements that the accused regularly wore an arm band indicating an association with the Red Cross did not constitute a new issue in the case which gave the Prosecution the right to a case in reply. When the Trial Chamber indicated yesterday that it was not minded to allow a case in reply upon this issue, the Prosecution sought leave to reopen its case in-chief, in order to call Witness VG117 upon this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask Your Honour to slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Groome for the Prosecution explained his failure to call this evidence at the proper time because he had not realised that the Defence witnesses would depart from their prior written statements when they gave their evidence and that he had eliminated VG117 from the Prosecution's witness list because, prior to the trial, the Trial Chamber had emphasised that there should not be any unnecessary proliferation of witnesses on the same issue and because VG117 had been reluctant to give evidence. The Trial Chamber, however, had also made it clear, prior to the trial, that it was not disposed to follow the practice of some Trial Chambers in the past of permitting the parties freely to present cases in reply and rejoinder without proper justification. A good illustration where the Trial Chamber made it clear that a case in reply was justified arose in relation to the evidence of Dr. De Grave for the Prosecution when Mr. Domazet failed to put the Defence case in contradiction of his evidence to him in cross-examination. The whole purpose of the introduction of Rule 90(H)(ii) requiring the cross-examiner to do just that is to prevent unnecessary cases in reply and rejoinder. Whether Mr. Groome is justified in the course he took is not a matter that needs to be resolved, as even if he were quite mistaken in taking that course, the fact remains that the evidence concerning the alleged representation by the accused that he was associated with the Red Cross, if accepted, may prove to be an extremely important part of the Prosecution case as to his knowledge that something untoward was to happen to the group from Koritnik once they were corralled in the houses in Pionirska Street. Mr. Domazet stated that he had evidence in response to the proposed evidence of VG117 from persons who were at the Vuk Karadzic School at the relevant time that the man who was registering people on behalf of the Red Cross was not the accused but another man who resembled him. Apart from denying the evidence of VG117, such evidence may have the effect also of reducing the probative value of the Prosecution witnesses who said that it was the accused who was offering the guarantee of safety on behalf of the Red Cross in Pionirska Street on the 14th of June, 1992. Such evidence would thus have been admissible in the Defence case. However, it is only fair that the accused should now be permitted to reopen his case to call such evidence once the Prosecution is permitted to reopen its case in chief to call VG117. There is therefore no prejudice to the accused caused by permitting the Prosecution to reopen its case for that purpose. The Trial Chamber does, however, emphasise that VG117 will be permitted to give evidence only in relation to the conduct of the accused at the Vuk Karadzic School, including the basis upon which she identified him. Mr. Groome has already conceded that evidence of the date upon which this is alleged to have occurred, which would otherwise have been very relevant to another important part of the Prosecution case, should not be given, although it would be reasonable to permit Mr. Groome to state that it was within so many days of the day upon which the house in Pionirska Street was burnt down, with a loss of so many lives. No other evidence will be permitted from VG117 in-chief which tends to corroborate or support the Prosecution case in any other way in relation to the accused's association with the death of these people in Pionirska Street or in relation to any other issue in the case. The cross-examination of VG117 cannot, of course, be so circumscribed as the Defence would unfairly be prejudiced by the reopening if it were prevented from eliciting from her any evidence in support of its case which it would have been able to elicit from her had she been called in the Prosecution case in-chief. However, if the cross-examination does stray into other issues, the Prosecution must, in turn, be entitled to deal further with those issues in the same way as it would have been entitled to deal with them had she been called in the Prosecution case in-chief. The Trial Chamber draws attention to that prospect so that the Defence does not inadvertently stray into other issues without realising what the consequences will be. One consequence of this ruling is that it may now be impossible for the Trial Chamber to complete the hearing of this trial by the end of next week as it had hoped to. Two members of the Trial Chamber are due to participate in another trial which commences on the 21st of January and which is expected to take a considerable period of time. I propose to make arrangements for this trial to continue in tandem with that other trial for a limited period. Such an arrangement will place a considerable burden on the Judges concerned as it means that they will be sitting in one trial starting in the early morning and the other in the afternoon and into the evening. It is therefore essential that everything in the present case which can be completed before the end of next week must be completed by then. This is an issue which can be discussed after the next witness has been called. Now, your next witness, Mr. Groome, I understand you want to get through today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the witness is scheduled. I was mistaken. It's an 8.00 flight this evening. So we have the entire day if we need him and that's Dr. Nigel Raby, and he's in the witness room and his computer has been set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness, the doctor will be working with some of the X-rays in a PowerPoint presentation. We attempted this morning to get copies for the Court, but because of some computer incompatibilities, that was not possible. What I'm proposing, that is, when he concludes his testimony, Mr. Bruff will take him down to the computer section and we will have copies for the Court to use in its deliberations of everything that he uses here in court today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, will you please make the solemn declaration in the document that the usher is handing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Morning, Dr. Raby.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dr. Raby, I ask you to begin by telling us what is your profession and where do you currently work.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I'm a radiologist, and I work at the Western Infirmary in Glasgow, Scotland.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what is your position there?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I'm a consultant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to briefly describe for us your post-graduate education.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I spent some time training in general physician -- as a general physician, obtaining a post-graduate degree of the so-called MRCP. That's the Medical Council Physicians of the United Kingdom. Subsequently then trained in radiology and obtained post-graduate qualification, and I'm a Fellow of the Royal College of Radiologists.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you briefly summarise your professional experience for us?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: My main experience professionally is in the radiology of trauma, damage to bone, muscles, and soft tissues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in addition to your -- well, in addition to what you've described, you also have some teaching responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes. I, with some colleagues, run a course done for some 13 years now which trains junior doctors in the interpretation of X-rays particularly relating to trauma. This is run a dozen times a year. We have about 1.200 students each year go through these courses. And consequent to that, there is a book published related to the course which has been in circulation for some years. It's now regarded as one of the base textbooks in the United Kingdom for such a subject and sold heavily in the United States and Australia, and is translated into several languages in addition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And are you one of the authors of that book?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I am indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In addition to that book, have you published articles in professional journals regarding the field and study of radiology?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Many articles, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, before we talk specifically about this case, I'm going to ask you to describe for us the basics of an X-ray plate and what it is we need to know about the fundamentals of it before we begin to study it and draw conclusions from it.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, a radiograph, as we call it, radiograph or X-ray, is obtained. Usually in the field of trauma, we obtain two radiographs taken at right angles to one another. This is important because you have a three-dimensional structure which you're trying to visualise in two dimensions, so one plate, one view taken either from the front or the side would be insufficient to ascertain the position of bones that have undergone trauma and displacement. The radiographic plate, bone simply stops X-rays reaching the plate and leaves the plate looking white. Soft issues and air allow X-rays to reach the plate and the plate turns black. So we see bones as essentially white structures, gaps between bones and structures around the bones as essentially black structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, just to clarify a little bit, I'm going to ask you to refer to the computer screen and I would direct or ask everybody in the courtroom to look at their computer screens. Would you put up the frontal or AP view of the bone and describe for us where the front of that bone is? When we talk about the front of the bone, can you maybe indicate where that is for us?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I'll need to flick a few screens forward here, if you bear with me. These lines will appear. We can come back to them later on. But if you want to look starting at the frontal bone, we'll just get past this and then we'll come on to this. That is a view of the frontal view. That's looking at the front of the leg. It's if the person was standing directly in front of you and you were looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps with your cursor you could show us on the right hand of the 2001 X-ray there, could you maybe drag the cursor along the front of the bone.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, the front of the bone would actually be down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've --

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Because that's facing towards you. So that's the front of it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Can I just clarify that? Remember that an X-ray is passing through the body from front to back. So what is superimposed on it is the back of the bone. So we're looking straight through from front to back.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the left side of the image of the bone, would it be fair to say that that is the side of the bone and not actually the front of the bone?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, in specifically now regarding this case, were you requested to examine a number of X-rays and to study them and to make a report on them?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I seek to tender Prosecution document number 166, the CV of Dr. Raby, and Prosecution Exhibit 169, the report of Dr. Raby.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I must have an early edition. It doesn't have numbers on the bottom. Is there any objection, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have fresh copies. They will be provided in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. The CV will be Exhibit P166 and the report dated the 12th of December, 2001 will be P167.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd ask you to return to your first slide, and I'll ask you a few questions about your conclusions. Before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I misread it. The report should be P169. I had written down the two consecutive numbers, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct, Your Honour. It's 169.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It is 169. I'm sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, before we actually get into your analysis, I want to ask you about -- can you describe for us in measuring distances on bones, or let's say on the tibia, did you choose a reference point from which you took all measurements?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you show us with your cursor where the reference point was?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: The reference point is the distal tibia, which is that point there, that structure there. It's a slight curve, but take the highest point. It's actually been marked there and you can also see on this other radiograph a similar point has been marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is there -- what is the scientific name for that part of the tibia?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: It's called the plafond.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you just to spell that for our reporters.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: It's p-l-a-f-o-n-d.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can you describe for us in measuring the distances on a fracture, or let's talk about this case specifically, how did you approach the task of comparing the two X-rays that were provided to you?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, having established that fixed reference point which was common to both radiographs, it's then possible to make comparable measurements from that distal point to the tibia to the various parts of the fracture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when the bone is fractured completely into two separate sections, does that impact from where you take measurements from?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: If there is some bony overlap, then it's possible to get slightly confused, but the way to overcome that is to make sure that you use the fixed portion of bone which isn't going to move. In this case, that's the lower portion of the bone, which is why we've taken the distal end of the bone as the reference point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to proceed to your next slide. Now, on the X-ray from 1992, did you take a measurement from the reference point to the lowest part of the fracture on the lower portion of the bone or the tibia?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would you tell us how it was you determined what the lowest point of the fracture was?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, if I take that arrow off one second and use my cursor again if it will come up, you can see, I hope, that we can see the -- this is the front of the bone. Remember we're looking side on at the leg now. So this is the front portion of the tibia, shin bone, and you can see it coming up to this point here at which point there is a black line going across. Now I'll just draw your attention to this structure here, which is the top half of the fracture as it were. This bone has actually overlapped and displaced slightly. So this -- you could say, Well, why don't I measure there? That's because it's not, in fact, physically at this moment attached to the bottom half because the bone has broken in two along this line here. So I can trace with confidence the front edge of this bone and I can follow it -- follow it to there where it should continue towards the top of the screen but then it stops, and at this point it goes off at an angle and, therefore, that's the distance from my fixed reference point on the front of the bone looking side on to the most proximal portion of the fracture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what was the measurement of that distance?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: That's 8 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please proceed to your next slide. Did you measure -- make a similar measurement on the X-ray plate from 2001?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us how you determined where the lowest portion of the fracture on that leg was?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if we do -- repeat the same exercise, now, this case, the fracture that is or has been clearly present in this bone is no longer visible as a black line because the fracture is united, but what you can see is the legacy of the healing process, which is this white substance. You can see here, normally, the centre of a bone is actually fairly dark but there is this white substance here, which is the way the body has healed across the fracture line. Therefore, this delineates where the fracture line was, and you can see it going down. And that process terminates at this point here, which is why I've made that measurement as the lower end of the fracture that has occurred in the past in this leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you measure that distance, what was it?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: This is only 4 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Raby, these are two different X-rays taken a number of years apart. Are there any problems with comparing the distances or the measurements on two X-rays that were taken by different machines at different times?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: There's a potential problem if the factors used to take the radiographs are substantially different. The main thing would be possible difference in magnification, but if one actually looks at the radiographs and looks at these bones, and particularly those of the ankle, which are actually slightly cut off the bottom of the right-hand image, these bones are virtually the same size. So in other words there is no major magnification factor at work here. If it is present, it is a matter of millimetres and therefore these two X-rays are, in fact, comparable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, would you please proceed to your next slide?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, remembering that you're calling this witness in reply, you would be entitled to put to him specifically the evidence given by the Defence witnesses which you have to deal with in some stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But you don't have to ask it in a non-leading form. You can put to him the witnesses' evidence about the calcification or whatever it was so that he can deal with it. You may want to do it after he's been through all of these slides, but at some stage you are entitled to put it to him directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I actually planned it a little later but if the Court finds it helpful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, no. The way you asked that last question was so carefully non-leading, I thought you might have been under a misapprehension that you were not allowed to ask it in a leading form.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you make a measurement from the reference point on the 1992 X-ray to what you determined to be the highest point on the fracture?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how did you determine where the highest point on the fracture was on the 1992 image?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: The process is exactly the same as for the -- as discussed previously. If I take this off, again our proximal reference point, bottom end, is the same, and again, what we are looking for is -- I have decided, determined, here is the fracture, here is the fracture line going here. I'm looking for the uppermost portion of that. And I can also confirm that that's the uppermost portion because I can also see this fragment of bone here, going up here, should actually marry with this piece here, but it doesn't because it's fractured and displaced and therefore is a portion of bone going to this point here, and that then marries with the fracture line that I've determined coming up at this point here. So there is the upper margin, which then fits in like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what did you calculate the distance between your reference points?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: That's 14.5 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you make a similar comparison or measurement on the X-ray from 2001?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you please move to your next slide? Can you describe for us how it was you determined on this healed bone where you believed the original fracture -- the highest point on the original fracture was located?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Again, a similar process. From our fixed reference point at the bottom, I have an idea of the approximate plane of the fracture from down here, and then I'm looking to see where the bone returns to normal. You can see here that this bone here is actually much whiter and thicker than, for example, its counterpart at the front and that there is a bulge in the bone, a step in the bone, and this is where the fracture has reached. It follows up that line to this point here. So I have two methods of identifying that that is the top end of the fracture which has now healed at that site, which gives me that line there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, before we move on to that, I want to ask you about this bump that you've described. Would it be fair to say that that is a result of the healing process or the remodelling process of the bone?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for us is there a standard way that the bone remodels itself or are there variations?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: There are variations, but they are relatively minor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us a little bit about the process of remodelling and the possible variations in what you would see on a healed bone?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, following a fracture, the body will try and immobilise the fracture site by laying down some tissue to try and stop movement and to try and help bone to form again across the fracture site, thereby repairing the bone. The technical term for that is callus. It's not true bone but it's a sort of primitive tissue. It does that to try and immobilise the bone, relieve pain and allow the bone to start healing. After a period of time, this substance called callus, which has served its purpose, starts to be reabsorbed by the body and that area replaced by new, healthy bone, as we would understand bone. As a result of that process, there is usually left telltale mark or sign where that process occurred. It's unusual for the process of a fracture, particularly if the fracture has initially been displaced somewhat, for that to occur with absolutely perfect match. So the body then undergoes this process which we describe of remodelling, remodelling that primitive callus tissue into healthy bone tissue. It's very rarely that it's an absolutely perfect alignment, so you end up with a little telltale bump or mark where that process has occurred. If the fracture is very severely displaced, and they are unable to get very good alignment, that may be a very major deformity that's left and signs left. If the fracture has been able to be pulled into good alignment with only a little bit of repair work done -- to be left to be done by the body, then that telltale sign will be relatively small.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this phenomenon that you're talking about now, how -- in distance, how far would it progress past the original fracture site? Can you give us a value of what the limits are?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I think it's difficult to give exact values, as I've said. It slightly depends on how displaced and how malaligned the fracture is. But a good, simple fracture with good alignment, you'd expect this to be a matter of one to two centimetres maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Looking at this particular X-ray from 2001, can you give us an opinion regarding how wide or how long this remodelation process, how far along the bone or how much of the bone does it occupy?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Looking at this, I don't think -- I think this bone has been in reasonably good alignment following the fracture and initial treatment, and that the extent of this remodelling would be fairly limited, and that therefore what we are seeing here as a legacy of that process is very close to the original fracture site.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So in other words, the bump that you've described, it's your belief that the fracture line is in the same proximity as that bone?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your opinion, is it possible that -- that the actual fracture line could be two to three centimetres below that bump or feature you described for us?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I think that's too far away. I think it would be less than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look below that bump that you've determined to be the highest point and ask you, do you see any feature along that bone that would indicate to you the possibility that the fracture terminated at a point lower than the point that you've selected?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did you measure this distance between, on the 2001 X-ray, from the reference point to the highest point of the healed fracture?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what value did you determine for that?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Twenty centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, doctor, we have been looking at the side or lateral view of the two X-rays from 1992 and 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you also conduct a similar exercise with the AP or frontal view of the X-rays?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to proceed to that slide. I'm sorry, before we go there, did you also trace the fracture on both of these X-rays?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you please show us the fracture in the 1992 X-ray?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I take that off and take you through that. As I described earlier, one has to determine where there is a break in the bone, and that is seen as this black or darker line extending to this point here, so the break is from there. Remember again, this is an overlap. This shadow here, this white structure here, is the top part of the bone which has been, as it were, displaced and forced down a little bit. So it may confuse you. I hope I'm making this reasonably clear. The fracture therefore starts there and goes through to that point there, like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Maybe if you would remove it and put it back one or two times to assist us. Could you now trace the fracture on the 2001 X-ray for us?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, again, we've -- as I've previously explained, I've determined the -- where the fracture line, I believe, lay at the front of the bone. Remember again, we are looking at the side, so this is the front. From this point here and it terminates at that point there. The line we can see of the repair and healing of bone through here, coming up here, and then there is a sort of long tongue projection up the back of the bone there, getting close to the point at the top, to give a fracture line of approximately that plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could you remove and put that back one or two times to assist us? Now, if we might move to the frontal or AP view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Before that happens, I wonder if you could get the doctor to explain this to me. When you compare the red line which he has showing the fracture, and the measurements he has taken, I'm just a little curious to know why the -- on the 1992 one, the measurement is taken from a point above the bottom of the fracture. I know why the doctor says that. But when he gets to the 2001, the fracture appears to end above where the measurement is taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you understand the Judge's question?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes. I've been trying to simply indicate the general plane of the fracture. The actual measurement I think you should take as the true extent of the fracture. I'm trying to indicate the degree of angularity and the overall length of the fracture indicative. I've not measured that. The red line has not been measured. It's been drawn by me freehand to just try and assist you in understanding the plane of the fracture, but it's not an accurate measurement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, let me ask you this. Let's look at the 2001 X-ray and the top of the yellow arrow that says 4 centimetres, there is a gap between that and where the red line terminates?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you explain --

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Again, the measurement -- the green and yellow lines are ones that I've accurately measured. The red line is simply a free-hand depiction by myself of the approximate plane of the fracture, to show that there is quite a difference in the steepness of the angle of the fracture. It does not represent an accurate measurement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Proceed to the frontal view. Now, let's start with the 1992 image. And if you would proceed to the first calculation that you made regarding that.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I should go through the process before. This is the fixed reference point, the bottom or distal end of the tibia, the tibial plafond which I defined earlier. This is the point which I use as a reference. 2001, similar point. Here again is the fracture. And again, you have this problem perhaps of not quite appreciating that there is a fracture line there and you say there is another line there. This is again due to the bone having overlapped. So to calculate, we again are going to use the distal portion, that's the bottom half of this bone, which is fixed to the ankle joint. This is the part which can move. So that would be inaccurate. So we can use the portion which doesn't move with reference to our distal point. If we trace up the margin of the bone and we get to the point here, then we see taking off is one line there and another line there. So that is the distance that I've measured from there to that point there, which is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I just ask you to retrace? You said that the bone took off in two directions. Could you just retrace the cursor a little bit slower to show us again?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: From this point, there are two lines that you can see. There is one line going across in this direction, which ultimately ends up going there, and there is another line going in that direction. Remember, this is a roughly circular, three-dimensional structure, so the fracture line -- one of these fracture lines is actually going around the front of the bone. Another one is passing around the back of the bone. It's doing it in a spiral fashion. So that they are forming different angles and passing in a different plane to finally meet at that bony spicule up there. So eventually, if you can imagine tracing around this as a circular object, you go along there, up there, around there, up to this point here, back down to -- this is the back of the fracture, if you like, and back where you started.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you -- just once again, can you trace what would be the front portion of the bone in this image?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Front portion in this image is this portion here. This you see would marry with this portion of the bone here, which is where the fracture has occurred, and this bone has overlapped. So this portion of bone here should in fact, in a normal person, be fitting into here, just slightly like a jigsaw. The two pieces would marry back together if we could get them into position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What did you calculate that measurement to be?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Eight centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you also take a measurement to the highest point on the fracture as you determined it?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let's move to the 2001.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: We can do it whichever way you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's do it in the order of your slides.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Okay. Similar process here, exactly the same as we did on the side-on view. Taking our fixed reference point, what we can see here again is this interruption of the normal appearance of the centre of bone, which is the telltale sign of where the body has had to heal the fracture, where the fracture line has, in the past, been passing across this point here and coming down to this point here. So there is the distance that I ascertained that was the lowest point of this fracture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what measurement did you find there?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Three centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Can we proceed to your next slide?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Again, would you describe for us how you determined or did you -- how did you determine the highest point of the fracture on the 1992 X-ray?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, if I take it off and show you again, taking our fixed reference point distally -- and again, I'm looking for -- this, as I explained just a minute ago, is slightly more complicated because it's describing a spiral around this bone, so what I've taken is where this line comes across and meets here, in fact then goes up the side of the bone and then there is another bony bit there. So on this view, I have decided to take this point here. There could be an argument for measuring there or there, but I've already used that as the highest point on the side-on view. I understand this is slightly difficult for you to understand but it's because it's a spiral injury in a circular structure which we are seeing in two dimensions. So I've ascertained -- and the reason that partly I've done there is because I can do the same comparable exercise on the other foot. But that is where I've decided -- I'll just clarify that. Where this line here, site of the fracture, comes across and meets the other side of the bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what did you calculate that to be?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Nine centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, before we move on, can you once again just point with your cursor to the highest point that -- the point that you did not choose, but the highest point of the fracture that we can see?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: There. It's a spicule of bone, a shard of bone, if you like, sticking out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, we are able to see that because the bones have dislocated; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: They have moved apart. Technically, it's not a dislocation. I don't think we should define a dislocation, but this, yes, the bone has fractured and has moved slightly apart, has angled, so that we can see that as a separate structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Assuming for a second that these were X-rays of the same leg, would you be able to see that same point on the image in 2001? Would you expect to see that?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: We would expect to see the telltale signs of bony remodelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the same --

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: On that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, did you make a similar calculation or comparison with the 2001 X-ray?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I did. And again, from my fixed distal point here, traced up the side of this bone, where there is again this telltale bump, as we described before, indicating that there has been bony remodelling here and that the fracture site is there or very close to that point, like so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What measurement did you get there?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: 11.5 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'd ask you to remove those -- the blue line and 11.5 centimetres, and I want to ask you something about the bump that you've observed. What would be -- in your expert opinion, what would be the maximum distance or variability of where the fracture, original fracture line could be from that bump or feature that you've observed on this bone?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Again because it's a relatively small bump, if we like to use that term, it implies that there has been a relatively small amount of callus formation and bony remodelling, which again suggests that the fracture site was close or very close to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, there are a couple of black lines at the top of the image. I know that you did not make them, but can you describe for us what you see when you look at that portion of the bone?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, what we're seeing here is just a tiny portion of the bony remodelling that we could see on the side-on view. The side-on view in that radiograph from 2001, if you may remember, the top-most portion of the fracture I'd ascertained as being some 20 centimetres from the distal joint. I don't think I can accurately measure it on this front view, but that's just sort of peeking out the side of this bone. But to see it properly is -- the best way to look at it is as we already have done, is from the side-on view.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in addition or as a result of this comparison of the measurements, do you have an opinion regarding whether or not the X-rays from 1992 and 2001 are of the same leg?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I have an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what that opinion is?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: It is not the same leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In addition to the measurements that you took, are there other features of the fractures and the heel fracture themselves which support your conclusion that they are not of the same leg?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- can I proceed to the next slide?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: If you take those lines off again, I think probably the most telling factor is that if we look at these fractures, so again if I draw your attention -- this is the main fracture line at the front of this radiograph. On this radiograph there is actually a healing fracture also going through here, again part of the spiral process so that, as in this one, you see one line there and one line there. On this one you can see one line healing through this point, and there's another line healing through that point. It's less easy for you to see, I appreciate. There is a little dent there which is again like the corollary of this bump here. In my opinion, that's where the fracture line was. Now, if I then mark those in for you, you have two fracture lines which appear superficially to lie in approximately the same position and plane. However, if we then look at the second component of these fractures, namely this one, you'll see in this one the longer and more vertical fracture lies above the red line, whereas on this fracture the longer and more vertical component of this spiral fracture lies below the red line. Clearly, that cannot have happened by any stretch of the imagination between this radiograph on your left and the radiograph on your right. Therefore, these are clearly radiographs of two different legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, earlier today did I ask you to take a white tube and to draw approximations of the fractures, of both fractures on the same tube?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask Mr. Domazet -- I gave it to Mr. Domazet to look at it. I'd ask if Mr. Domazet would give it to the usher and it be provided to the witness. If I could just see it before it's given to the witness. Perhaps we'll call this Prosecution artefact 172.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, did you trace as best you are able the fracture line that you observed from the two radiographs taken in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Maybe I'd ask you to just hold that up above the computer screen so the Court can see. What colour did you do that in?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: 1992 is in black.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: How is the front of the bone indicated on that tube?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: By the letter "F".

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you also trace the fracture or the healed fracture that you observed in the 1992 X-ray?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What colour did you do that in?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: That's in red.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do those two lines correspond?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd also note -- did you put your name and the date on that tube?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender Prosecution artefact 172 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit P172.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, just so that it's clear to those of us who may look at this tube, is it a scale representation?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: No. I'm no great artist. It's the best I can do, but I think it's fairly close to what we're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in addition to your examination of the fracture, did you make observations or comparisons between other parts of the bones depicted in the two radiographs?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could you please describe for us what you did -- what comparisons you made?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, these are radiographs labelled from 1992 and 2001 of the heel bone and associated bones around it taken from the two radiographs we've already been looking at. And one can compare the appearances of these bones to see if there are any major differences, and I found several. If I can draw your attention to the appearance of the bone here. This is call the talus, and at the back here it articulates with this bone here which is -- you've called the heel bone. Technically, it's the calcaneus. And you can see the rather globular configuration. It's a rounded structure. I hope you can appreciate that. If you take the same bones, here is the talus, here is the heel bone or calcaneus, and here is the portion that I'm interested in. You can think -- see this has a rather sharp and angulated, thin appearance as compared to this thick, globular, rounded appearance of the bone here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, it has been suggested to the Chamber by another expert, Dr. Vucetic, that over the course of the nine years between the taking of these two X-rays that a bone has -- it is normal for a bone to undergo deterioration and regeneration, and in this process of deterioration and regeneration that one would expect to find differences such as this between X-rays taken of the same bone nine years apart. Would you agree with that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I don't agree with that conclusion, not in this instance. There may be some truth in what he says about certain bones at certain sites, particularly after trauma, but this is a bone away from the trauma site. It's not a bone which is known to change its appearance particularly through life. It's a bit like having blue eyes or grey hair or whatever. That's kind of in your genes, and that's the way the bone forms. Everybody is a little bit different, and there is no reason to suggest that these bones should change their shape like this at this site.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is there another or are there other features which you found to be different --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Before you leave that one, Mr. Groome, I'm having a little trouble perceiving where we're referring to. If you look at the 1992 one on the screen and near the red arrow, there is a rounded shape which goes down over a darker area and then comes back over a lighter area. Now, is that the one that the doctor is referring to? Keep going. Yes, that's the one I'm referring to. Now, if you compare that to the 2001, is there not a similar shape coming down through the other bone? There seems to be some sort of a shadow of something there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the point here, I have the advantage of knowing the detailed anatomy of this area, but what you can hopefully see is this white line here which comes up to there and is continuous with that. This is actually on the other side of the bone. Again, this is a three-dimensional structure, so left and right, as it were, would be superimposed one on the other. But I can see this runs in continuity with this portion here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, there are --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And this side, if I do the same thing, I get to here. This white line comes up here and runs in continuity with this portion here. This white line continues on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So the shape that I can see in the 2001 is on the wrong side of the ankle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shape there is actually present here. It's that shape there. It's on the other side of the bone now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now could I ask you this then, Doctor -- I'm sorry, Mr. Groome, but I want to get this very clear in my mind. On 2001 where the red arrow is, is that almost like a spur there that comes out? It's very faint.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a little spur that comes out at that point there, just there, yes, which is not present on the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that the part that you're referring to though, Doctor? That's what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The overall -- yes. That's part of what I'm referring to. But the overall configuration is of a thin, almost sharp tongue of bone here, whereas here I've got a globular, rounded, much larger protrusion of bone there. There is this second portion here which is, if you like, on the other side of the heel, away from us, which marries with that there. But I'm concerned that this portion here does not have anything similar on this radiograph to that portion there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I now understand what the part of the bone was that you're referring to. I am sorry to have interrupted, Mr. Groome, but I didn't want to lose it before we went on to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, is there another feature that you compared between the two bones?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes. Again, there's this little bony excrescence here, which if you compare it with its counterpart on this again similar sort of process, this is a relatively small little bump here, whereas on here we have a much bigger, rounded bump. And again that's different, and there's no reason why that should particularly change with time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are these the two most significant differences that you found in the heel structures and the foot structures between the 1992 and the 2001 X-rays?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, I've highlighted these two as I'd hope that they were the two easiest for non-technical people to appreciate. There are some others which I can try and demonstrate to you if you would like.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to go through each of those now.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, if we look at the 2001 film, if we -- this is the back of the heel bone, and we can see that there's quite a big bump here as this comes out and round. This is a very thick white piece of bone. Unfortunately in this, and this is why I have not highlighted it particularly, I can actually see that this is different at this point here but I have to confess it is obscured by this wire support frame. So I may have difficulty in persuading you that that is a major difference. However, if I move on to this area here, I hope you may appreciate that there are a series of white lines running vertically, probably one, two, three, four, five -- five or six. The similar portion of bone here, there is, at most, one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, can you tell us what those white lines are?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: This is part of the internal structure of the bone. If you remember and appreciate that when we take an X-ray, we see the bone. So you don't see the skin overlying it. So you can see the bone, but the X-ray keeps going. So you're actually looking at the internal architecture of the bone. This is like the internal scaffolding. So there are struts, very fine struts of bone inside the bone. As you can see, it is a solid object, which are the internal scaffolding. These are called bony trabeculae, if I can indulge you with that Latin term, but that's the technical term. Think of it as scaffolding struts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you spell "trabeculae" just for the court reporter?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes, I can. T-r-a-b-e-c -- no. I have to write it down. I'm sorry. I'm getting mental lock. I can do it, but it's one of these long words. I can do it. T-r-a-b-e-c-u-l-a-e.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, Doctor, would a trabeculae, would one expect that to change significantly over the course of nine years in the same person?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: No, you would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are there any other features that you examined?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: On the same theme, you can also see here the supporting scaffolding of these trabeculae. Now, in this case in 1992, they radiate fairly uniformly from a line along here, this white line here, radiating out towards the back of the heel bone. If you look in this case here, the white line isn't nearly as distinct, but the way these radiate out, not in the same pattern, they actually form two sort of groups. There's one group which is going back in this sort of direction, and there's another direction which actually curve down towards this point. Now, as I say -- I appreciate that may be a -- slightly difficult to appreciate to those who are not used to looking at these things, but to recap, I'm trying to say that these come in a rather more uniform radial pattern whereas these form two distinct groups, one rather straight and one rather curved. I don't know if that can be appreciated or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, in addition to everything that you've compared so far, did you also compare the tibia -- I'm sorry, the fibula that's apparent in both X-rays?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to maybe flip back to one of your earlier images that will allow you to tell us your conclusions regarding that. Can you first tell us what you observe when you look at the tibia of the 1992 bone?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: It's normal. There is no evidence of injury -- sorry. To the fibula.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, to the fibula.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: The 1992 film, the fibula is entirely normal. There's no evidence of fracture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, what do you see when you look at the fibula on the 2001 X-ray?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: There is evidence of a healed fracture of the lower third of the fibula.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask you to maybe trace one or two times with your cursor to show us where you believe the fracture was on the fibula.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: It's in this area here. On this radiograph it doesn't show quite so well. In reality, in life, I have the advantage of what is known as a bright light where I can put the radiograph against a very bright light and show up that dark area of the radiograph. I haven't got the capacity to do that here, but on the original radiograph that's approximately where the fibula fracture is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If these two X-rays were of the same person, looking at the remodelation or the body's repair of the fibula in the 2001 X-ray, would you expect to see -- be able to see that fracture on the 1992 X-ray if it were the same person?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, it has also been at issue in this matter what impact a refracture approximately a year or slightly less would have on the ability to compare -- make the comparisons that you've made. So I would ask you, would you describe for us what, if anything, what impact would it have if a person suffered a refracture of the bone approximately three centimetres below the original fracture of the tibia approximately one year later?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that hypothesis can be answered because I don't think it would be able to refracture the bone three centimetres away from the original fracture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe for us why you think that is not possible?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, if you're going to refracture, the obvious place for the refracture to occur would be at the original fracture site. There is a theory that sometimes fractures unite and are even stronger than original bones so the fracture won't occur there, and there is some truth in that. So what would actually happen is that a refracture, if another injury was sustained, would occur well away from the fracture. So I think there's only two possibilities that could occur if the patient sustained another similar spiral type injury. They would either refracture exactly through the original fracture site or they would sustain another injury to this bone at some great distance, but I don't believe it's possible to have a second injury very close to the original fracture.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Looking at the two X-rays that you looked at, is it possible that a refracture of the bone approximately one year later accounts for the differences in measurements and angles that you have seen?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: No, I don't believe that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In course -- in the course of your work in this case, did you have an opportunity to read the report of Dr. Yvan De Grave?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would you please comment on his findings and methodology that he used?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: His methodology I felt was extremely sound and basically his findings and mine concur.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to look at the report of Dr. Vucetic?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you please comment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There are two reports, remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the two reports of Dr. Vucetic, one in November of last year and one in December of last year.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would you please comment on the methodology and the findings in his report?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: There wasn't so much methodology but the findings I disagreed with because his measurements and his comments about the type of measurements I thought were erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Groome, he is called in reply. Is he -- are you not going to ask him to explain why they are erroneous?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Particularly the effect of the callus formation on the ability of measure and the fact that even Dr. Raby's measurements differ according to which view you're looking -- which view he looks at the X-ray, and they certainly differ amongst each other. That's the purpose of calling him as a witness in reply, if I may suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you please comment for us on the differences or the reason, as you understand it or believe it to be, the differences between the measurements that each of the experts who have examined these X-rays have come to?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: From memory, I think the most obvious problem that they have is to say why is it that a measurement taken on one view, a front view, is a different measurement on the side view. Well, that's because it's a spiral fracture. So where you see -- if you look at the image in front of you on the left-hand side, for example, I'll try and explain this part. Again imagine this is our fracture line, so on this frontal view, I'm taking it on the one side of it to be there because that's where it crosses the bone there, on the other side to be there, because that's where it crosses the bone there. So that gives me two measurements on that view. Now, if I look at this bone side on, I'm going to be looking at this portion of the bone, right up the centre. Therefore, where I see the break in that bone on the side-on view will actually be probably about there and that will give me a different measurement, therefore, from that distance and a different measurement from that distance. The fracture is spiralling around the bone. So it simply depends on which angle you view the bone from. In fact, if you were to take, say, ten X-rays at 20 degree intervals going around the bone, every time where you measured the fracture line appeared to you, it would change. So it is not at all surprising that the measurements on one view are not the same as on the other view. In fact, that's entirely what you'd expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were you able to determine how Dr. Vucetic chose the point that he measured from?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I don't, because he provided no diagrams such as were provided with the other reports. He just made statements and gave measurements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Vucetic, one of the measurements that he calculated was the distance from the same reference point that you used, but he calculated the distance between that and the lowest portion of the upper part of the tibia that was broken that had overlapped. In your opinion, is that a sound way to measure and compare fractures?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: No. It makes no sense whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And why does it make no sense?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Because to treat the fracture, you're going to place the bones under traction and move them apart and back to their normal position. Therefore, the distance between the fixed distal reference point and the part of the fracture that he is measuring is subsequently then going to move by several centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Vucetic also talked about that callus formation or the remodelation of bone made it very difficult to have any reliable findings regarding measurements on the 2001 X-ray. What would be your opinion of that assertion?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I don't think that's the case. I mean, we can see where the bone remodelling has occurred. We can see the telltale signs of the approximate fracture line and the two coincide. So that to suggest that the callus or the remodelation, as you call it, is not closely approximated to the fracture line, again makes no sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And accepting, however, that assertion, would it explain the differences that you found between the two bones, the two X-rays?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: No. I don't think it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Raby. On behalf of the Defence, I shall have a few questions for you. First of all, relating to the fracture itself and the possibilities of healing. In any situation when a fracture heals, is the fracture line always visible?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes, almost certainly it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If that is so, how then can we tell that the fracture has healed?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: We can tell because we can see, as the example in front of you shows, that the two fragments of bone are not absolutely now perfectly aligned, but we can see that there is normal bone growth across that area. And we can also tell, in the real world, by clinically examining the patient, which is actually as important as looking at X-rays.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So your opinion is that on the radiograph of 2001, this fracture line is visible. I mean, the whole fracture line.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I can see where the fracture was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Once a fracture has healed, can the fracture itself be seen or the newly formed bone, the callus?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Newly formed bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This newly formed bone tissue or callus, does it merely fill in the gap or crack, or does it cover the area of the fracture, thickening the bone?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: It covers the area of the fracture and may thicken the bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This bone thickening, is it visible on a radiograph?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Judging by this thickening visible on radiographs, do we use them to orientate ourselves regarding the place, the location, of the fracture, or do we see the fracture line on the healed fracture?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: You can see both, because you can see the line of the healed fracture. You don't see the fracture itself because it's filled in, but you see where the filling in of the fracture has occurred, and you also see the remodelling of the bone around that site.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In that case, in your opinion, is it possible to have such precision regarding the appearance of the fracture after it has healed?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes, I think you can be quite precise where the fracture was, once healing has occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And in view of the years that have gone by after the original fracture, how do these years affect the site of the fracture? Does this have an effect regarding the degree of difficulty in determining the fracture site?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Not really. In good circumstances, complete healing will have occurred at about six months, and after that time, there will be very little or no subsequent change. The interval of another year, five, 10 or 20 years are unlikely to change the radiograph any further from about six months after the original injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you were answering Mr. Groome's questions regarding the fibula, when asked whether it is possible for the fibula to have been broken or cracked in 1992 without that being visible on the x-ray, I think that you said that that was impossible or highly improbable.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yesterday, Dr. Vucetic showed us radiographs of another case, with views of the fibula from two angles showing that on one of those angles, the fracture could not be seen, whereas on the other view it was visible. Would you agree that that was possible?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: That is in general possible, but not in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the case of a refracture, Mr. Groome's questions referred to a possible refracture three centimetres away from the original fracture. This is a figure that was given by the accused himself, Mitar Vasiljevic, who had heard from the doctors that the refracture was three centimetres away. However, if we put aside that figure, which need not at all be reliable, and we have medical documentation to show that 11 months after the original injury, there was a refracture, does a refracture, as a term, imply a fracture at the same site, a repeated fracture at the same site?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: A refracture, in my understanding, would mean a fracture through the original fracture line, not another fracture close to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I thought. So in your opinion, a refracture is a repeated fracture at the same site as the previous one.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said a moment ago, answering a question from Mr. Groome, that at times, this refracture - at least that was the term translated to me - was greater than the first fracture, larger, more significant. Could you explain what you mean? Does it mean a more serious fracture or what exactly you meant?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I said it was a greater fracture. I said if you had a second fracture, it may be further away, away from. But I don't believe I said that it would be a greater fracture, and if I did say that, that's not what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So very well. Let me refer to what you just said, that it was further away from the first fracture. Could you explain a little what that means?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, as I think I tried to explain earlier, if you are going to have a second fracture - by a second fracture I mean a different fracture at a different site, so not a refracture, which is another fracture through the original site - if you're going to have a second fracture, you will do one of two things, either go through the original site, which would be a refracture, or a second fracture would most likely occur well away from the site of the original injury. So in this case, where we can see the fracture is in the lower part of the bone, a second fracture would most likely occur in the upper part of the bone, in fact not even on the X-rays that we have here. It would be higher up the leg than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But there are no such traces on the radiograph of 2001?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In view of the medical documentation that we have saying that, in May 1993, Mitar Vasiljevic had a second fracture, and you have radiographs taken in 2001, would it be possible to conclude that that refracture from 1993, that is following the one of which you are looking at the X-ray from 1992, left the kind of traces that are now visible on the radiograph of 2001?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please explain why not? Do you mean that the refracture was absolutely identical to the 1992 fracture and that is why you have such an opinion, or is there some other reason for it?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, the measurements that I've given you between the first and second radiograph are quite different. The angles of the fracture are quite different, and in particular, on the radiographs that were still up on the screen, as I showed you, the orientation of the short versus the long fractures are entirely opposite to one another. I have already said that it would not be possible to have a second fracture at the same site, because you would either refracture, in which case the overall appearances, second radiograph would match the first, which they clearly don't, and so, as I say, it is not possible that there has been a second fracture at the site. You say you have medical documentation to say this has occurred. I think we would need to see the radiographs to show the second fracture and compare it with the first at that time, and I would be very happy to look at these if they were available.
