utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you refer to a radiograph, you mean a 1993 radiograph of the second fracture? I assume that is what you mean.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: If that's when the second fracture is alleged to have occurred, then that's when I would like to have a radiograph of, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but my question was: The radiograph of 2001, on which there are traces, visible traces, of a fracture, is it possible to establish, on the basis of that radiograph, whether there was a refracture or not?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: In my opinion, the radiograph of 2001 has evidence of one fracture. I see no reason to suggest that there has been two fractures on this radiograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the event that in 1992, and in 1993, there was a leg fracture at the same site, would it be possible to establish that in 2001? Would there be any difference, or would you just see a single, healed fracture, particularly bearing in mind the nine-year time interval?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I would see evidence of probably a single, healed fracture. The evidence that I have in front of me is that the radiograph of 2001 does not represent the fracture that is visible in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When commenting a moment ago on Dr. Vucetic's report, you said that he did not provide any images or sketches or drawings. However, yesterday, he did bring some drawings, which have been admitted into evidence, and I'd like you to look at them, as we are having a break now, and then we can comment on them after the break. This will give you a chance to look at them during the break, if the Prosecution hasn't already shown them to you before you started your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Were they admitted in evidence, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. As long as they are exhibits, then the doctor may have a look at them. What was the number, do you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, they were certainly in evidence. I'm sorry, I thought you were also referring to the X-rays that the -- that Dr. Vucetic had of another patient demonstrating the --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- fact that the regrowth or the remodelling had masked the original injury. You don't want him to have a look at those? Because I don't think they were put in evidence, were they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Yes, 38, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, Exhibit 38. Do you want him to look at those as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. Those may be shown to the doctor during the vacation -- during the adjournment. We will -- yes, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a brief scheduling matter. Dr. Broeders should be here by now. I anticipate that's going to take 15 or 20 minutes to switch this computer equipment with Dr. Broeders' audiovisual equipment that he has, just so that the Court knows. I don't know if the Court wants us to just put him on in the afternoon and finish possibly early in the morning session, or whether the Court wants to take a break in the middle of the morning session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just in case Dr. Raby wants to refer to this, I think we should keep this on the screen, and if necessary we will take a break while it's being done. We will resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Raby, I hope that you were able, during this break, to take a look at the evidence I've referred to provided by Dr. Vucetic.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to also read the supplemental report by Dr. Vucetic which was not available to you at the time when you gave your first opinion? And in it, there is also a table provided by him.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I have read that, but I don't have access to it to refer to at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What is its exhibit number? 29.1, is that the -- or 29? Because the doctor could be given the original exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think that it is D38, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: 38 was the Vucetic report, and actually, the court deputy was just telling me before we came in that it doesn't seem to have ever been handed in as an exhibit. It was made Exhibit 38, D38. So we'll need a copy of it anyway, but do you have a copy that you can show Dr. Raby?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have in mind the one dated 28th December of 2001? Is that what we have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I have in -- I haven't got the document in front of me either, but I'm thinking of the one that he sent, we received during the court vacation and in which he talked about the different measurements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have a copy handy if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, Mr. Groome. Do you have a number on it by any chance so that we can resolve --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have the original filing. I have the original filing, not the --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I can give a copy also. I can give a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I wasn't sure that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: As long as there are no secret messages in it, Mr. Domazet. That's all we were worried about. That was a joke.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The first two pages of the supplemental report contain an explanation of Dr. Vucetic, and on the third page there are matters that I consider to be relevant and that I would like Dr. Raby to comment since he has been brought here to rebut this very evidence. Dr. Vucetic, in the supplemental report of his, mentions the determination of the upper spot of the fracture of tibia on the profile X-ray dating from 1992, and he finds that your measurement was 14.5 centimetres. Dr. De Grave's measurement was 15.2, and Dr. Bollen's 13 centimetres. And he believes all these variations to be significant and believes that they need to be explained. The reasons for them could be a different methodology used in interpretation of the X-rays. Dr. Vucetic's measurement was 15.4. This pertains to the upper spot. Could you comment on this, please?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, I think -- if I can look at these images so I can remind myself exactly what we're looking at. I have the thing off. So this is on the -- just remind me, 2001 or 1992? 1992, I think you said.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, as I pointed out to you earlier, there is a degree of interpretation as to where you actually define the fracture line to end. It seems to me that the differences in those measurements are actually very small and probably not significant. Surely of more significance is the comparative between the approximate same distance in 2001, where there is quite a degree of difference between the two. It's really that that matters rather than the very small differences in the measurement of the single film by different people dated at the same date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. We will get to the 2001 X-ray. However, this that I referred to pertained to the X-ray of 1992, which is much more clear and can be more easily used to determine things than the one from 2001. Now, as we speak of the X-ray from 1992, the values for the lowest point differ in a very small degree, some three to four millimetres, so this cannot be constituted as significant, but in the X-ray of 2001, using the same view, Dr. Vucetic found that this spot was at some four centimetres, which cannot be really viewed clearly but is interpreted as the final point of the fracture healing. Dr. Vucetic's measurement was 5.5 centimetres. And this has been explained in this table that you perhaps have in front of you, and all of the differences in various measurements have been entered into this table, so I would like to hear your comment regarding this.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: He has provided me with some diagrams to show where he may have measured to, although I'm just a little confused because the diagram is of a right leg but we are examining a left leg. I guess I could just invert the image. Having said that, he labels four points, some of which relate to the overlap of bone, but it's not clear to me which of the four points he's used for his measurements, although he's labelled them and signified that they exist. I can't at this moment see where he's chosen to measure them because he's given figures but doesn't say which of the points he actually used for his measurements. So I'm a little confused as to exactly where he took the measurements from. But I suspect that that's one of the explanations for his different values that he has taken, and as I explained to you earlier in the morning, it's the bottom part of the bone that's attached to the ankle and therefore not going to move that I believe should be used. And I think the other experts have come up with similar figures to mine also believe should be used, and I have a feeling that he may have used measurements from the fixed distal point, which I've already indicated, to the bottom end of the fracture in the top part of the bone, which, as I also explained, is overlapped and therefore the distances are different, and therefore I would suspect that in fact represents erroneous methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When we talk about the upper point of the tibia fracture, the point where it has healed in the X-ray from 2001, according to you, it was determined to be 20, and Dr. Bollen determined it to be 20.3 centimetres. You can see in front of you the opinion of Dr. Vucetic, which states that the point that you took to be the upper point of the fracture is in fact a trace of a healed fracture, and that according to him, fracture can be seen in the part -- in the middle part, in the central part of the bone, and the cortex of the bone shows thickening of the newly created bone, which took place when the bone healed, and this is linked to the cortex at a distance of a few centimetres from the fracture. He proceeds to explain - and you can see that on page 3 of the opinion which is in front of you - that this thickening and the callus is especially manifested in the fractures which were treated in the way that Mr. Vasiljevic's fracture was treated, by immobilisation and various -- and tractions. And because of that, Dr. Vucetic believes that this point that you determined to be 20 centimetres is a trace of a healed fracture, and that that point, which can be seen radiographically as a change in the bone cortex, is not the trace of the fracture line. He believes the fracture line to be lower and to be readily visible on the X-ray. He believes that it is at 16.5 centimetres from the lower point of tibia. Can you comment on this assertion of Dr. Vucetic expressed in the supplemental report as well as yesterday in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I think I can take some comfort that Dr. De Grave, Dr. Bollen and I come to virtually identical conclusions and identical figures. I don't really think it's for me to explain why the last gentleman in this list has come to a completely different figure. I don't really understand how he's come to that. An explanation of callus around the fracture site extending - he would then have to say by three and a half to four centimetres - in a fracture of this type is really an untenable argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since you are talking about measurements, it is true that in this table, we can see that Dr. De Grave's and Dr. Bollen's measurements are the same. I would just like to remind you that Dr. De Grave in fact used the expert opinion of Dr. Bollen. We know that Dr. De Grave is not a radiologist, so he accepted somebody else's measurements. It is also true that the differences between all of you are small. However, the explanation of Dr. Vucetic that I just read concerning the thickening of the bone wall and what you see at 20 centimetres is only the healing of the fracture and not the beginning of the fracture line is basically the substance of the differences in your opinion.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, that is the substance, and I think that measurement made on that basis is wrong. I believe that the line we can see, that the bump in the cortex represents where the fracture ends or very, very close to it, certainly nothing like four centimetres short of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, it is not four centimetres. You yourself have said that there can be variations of one to two centimetres. And here, if we were to accept the upper point used by Dr. Vucetic, the variation would be three and a half centimetres. But it can definitely not be the upper point used by you and measured by you to be 20 centimetres, and this is where the difference lies. I would like for you to look at the table in front of you, and when we are discussing the frontal X-ray of tibia dating from 1992, the lower fracture line of tibia -- the lower fracture point of tibia is, according to Dr. Bollen, five centimetres. Dr. De Grave didn't discuss this. And you believe this to be eight centimetres, which you will certainly admit is a significant difference. Is this difference caused by measuring different points or is there another explanation to it? Could you please explain?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I think I mentioned earlier I think what's probably happening here is that they're measuring the part of bone sticking down furtherest of the top part of the fracture whereas I confined myself to the fixed bottom part of the fracture.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The X-ray from 2001, the frontal view of it, the lower point of the fracture is measured by Dr. Bollen as being three centimetres and 3.9 centimetres in the profile view. Do you think it is contradictory because these two projections should be showing the same image?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: No. As I explained earlier, when you look from side on, you're not seeing the same point of the fracture as when you're looking front on. It's spiralling around the bone. And if the two measurements were the same, that would actually be quite unusual. So the difference in measurements is exactly what one would expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As far as your measurement of that same point is concerned, and now we're talking about the X-ray from 2001, does this apply or the difference is even greater? In the front view, you measured it to be three centimetres, and in the lateral view four centimetres. So there is a one centimetre of difference. And could we say that it is difficult to determine the fracture line of a fracture after nine years have passed?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I don't think the differences are significant. I think that demonstrates where the fracture line is with reasonable accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Your measurement of the upper point of the fracture line in the frontal view of an X-ray from 1992, you measure it to be 9 centimetres and 14.5 centimetres for the same point in the lateral view. And when we compare these measurements, there should be the same point used in both frontal and lateral view of the X-ray from 2001. Dr. Vucetic finds completely different values for the upper point of the fracture. In the frontal view, it is 11.5 centimetres, and 20 centimetres in the lateral view. He believes this to be impossible. Can you comment on this as well, please?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I think it's the same explanation as I've given you. It's a separate view of a spiral fracture, and if the two were the same, it would be unusual. We would expect them to be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Don't you believe -- don't you think that these differences are far too significant, great?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the supplemental report on page 6, there is a comment of Dr. Vucetic, and he uses three points. I will read this to you, and I will ask you to comment on this. He believes that you are not using the same points in your measurements and that the points should be the same in frontal and lateral view both in 1992 and 2001 X-rays.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Sorry, can you just say that again? The points on the 1992 and 2001 should be the same. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, not myself. Dr. Vucetic is saying that, yes, that in order to determine the same points, it should be -- they should be the same, that you are not measuring the same points in frontal and lateral view and that the lateral view is done in the event of fractures in order to determine the same points and that this is the only way to identify them in different views.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, the whole point of doing two views is to identify different points, not the same point. If you only had to see the same point, then you wouldn't need to take two views. The second view is to determine the configuration of the fracture which will not be visible on one view. So that if you were to take one view here, you would be very erroneous in fully appreciating the extent of this fracture. So that when you take a side-on view after the frontal view, you get some separate measurements which actually clarify the extent, the size of the fracture, the length of the spiral, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but in this case, this is a fixed point from which you start. Dr. Vucetic also finds that the lower point of the fracture on the 1992 X-ray was fixed in both views at the same level of eight centimetres, so please correct me if I'm wrong. And that in both views you measured the same points. But that is not the case with the other measured points on the 1992 X-ray and the 2001 X-ray.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: It just so happens that on one of these measurements the appearance or the site of the fracture on the side view and the frontal view coincide. That's actually quite unusual. We would not expect them, in the majority of cases, to do so. So the one that actually has the same measurement is not to do with the same point, because the lateral view is giving you a separate view and the side-on view is giving you a separate view to the front view, and you would not expect to be measuring the same point. You're seeing the fracture from a different perspective. So you will have different points to measure to from your fixed reference point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Regarding the fracture line, a spiral fracture - and this is not in dispute - in what way did you determine the angle, in view of the fact that a spiral fracture takes the form of a letter "S", so to speak, so that there are different angles?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct. So if you were to attempt to take, say, ten radiographs around the leg at various angles, you would see a different angle for the fracture at every site. We take two, by convention, because that generally suffices to give us the information that we need. So you can determine the angle as it appears, which may not be exactly as it is, as it appears on the front view, and you can take and measure an angle as it appears on the lateral view, the side view. It's not -- the angle in terms of treating the patient that we perceive there is not -- is not particularly crucial. So it's not important that we determine the minutiae of the angle of the spiral to determine the treatment of the patient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think, Doctor, what Mr. Domazet is seeking to put from Dr. Vucetic's evidence is it may not be important for the purposes of treatment, but for the purposes of comparison, when one party is saying it is the same person and the other is saying it cannot possibly be the same person, it has some relevance, does it not? That's, as I understand it, what is being put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And I think we've previously, I hope, shown where I've drawn the angles from, how I've determined where the fracture sites were and shown the comparison between the two and shown that they're really quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On the last page of the report that you have before you, Dr. Vucetic indicated six of his conclusions in summary form. This is on the last page. So would you be kind enough to look at them and comment on them? Because after all, they are conclusions of an expert witness whose testimony you are rebutting today. And if you could tell us which of these points you may agree with and which you disagree with, and if you disagree with them, why you disagree with them?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Okay. Point 1, he states it's not possible to establish the previous appearance of a healed fracture based on a radiograph taken nine years following healing. I would disagree. I think it is possible. I think I've shown that to be the case. We can see the legacy of the fracture. We can see where the callus formation has been and the remodelling has occurred. We can see the extent of the fracture. The fact that it's nine years is no more important than if it was nine months. In that intervening period, it would have changed very little since, and in ten years from now, it will have changed very little since. So that period of time is not particularly important. Point 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [In English] One moment, doctor, please. [Interpretation] Point 1, you said it was not possible. Dr. Vucetic said it was not possible in detail. He didn't say that it was not possible at all but simply that it was not possible to establish in detail. After all, that's not quite the same, is it?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I think we can establish to within a few millimetres, if not more than a centimetre, where the original fracture lay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. I was just pointing out that Dr. Vucetic didn't say that it was not possible to establish but that it was not possible to establish in detail. So that's fine now, and I apologise for interrupting you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Point 2, he states that determination of the upper and lower fracture points is varying in individual measurements in each expert, in both the AP, which is the frontal, front-on, and the lateral, which is the side-view, radiographs in 1992 and 2001. I think we've discussed this and shown that there are various points one could take to measure. I've explained why I've chosen mine. They accord with certainly one if not two of the other experts, and disagree with one. And I think I've explained why those discrepancies may occur, namely the overlapping and shortening of bone and using the upper portion as a measurement site, which, in my opinion, is erroneous. So I think that's an explanation for point 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you have any comments to make regarding the other points of these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Point 3, he says that the values measured are significantly different. I think we've looked at several of the measurements and found that they are remarkably similar. There are one or two that differ and I've explained, partly on the basis of the previous answer, why they may differ.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That probably also applies to point 4. Could you please comment on point 5 as well?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: He says that it is possible by traction to correct the bone length shortening at the fracture site, which can result in an enlarged distance measured between the limiting points of the fracture line from the upper to the lower part of the bone. Well, that actually doesn't make any sense whatsoever because the whole purpose of traction is to replace the two ends of bone together, like a jigsaw puzzle, back to where they should originally be, and as I have measured the fixed portion of the bone which doesn't move in this process, if the top part is replaced on the bottom part, then that traction process should not affect any of the measurements that I have made whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Finally, Doctor, since I received your detailed CV a moment ago, but it can clearly be seen that you're an expert radiologist, my question is: In your practice so far, how frequently have you encountered orthopaedic patients?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Probably 50 or 60 patients per day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. In view of this number, I must ask you, then, how many patients you have daily as a whole.

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: I'll clarify the word "patients." Remember, as a radiologist, I don't generally see patients. I see the X-rays or the scans of various types of patients. Between 9.00 and 11.00 on every weekday, I will report fractures of bones in approximately 30 to 40 patients. Throughout the rest of the working day, I will then report on various types of scans using various types of radiological equipment on a further 20 to 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So what you are telling us is really viewing the X-rays of those patients; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But in your practice, have you had occasion to actually directly follow the treatment of trauma patients with fractured bones? Have you participated in that treatment in any way at any orthopaedic clinic?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: No. It is not the role of radiologists to do that. No radiologist in the world does that. We do follow the radiographs and are consulted by our orthopaedic surgeons to discuss with them the findings on the radiographs, but we rarely see the patients. It's not our role.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, doctor. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Doctor, before the break, Mr. Domazet made some reference to two different views of a leg that Dr. Vucetic brought with him, which were never put into evidence. My question to you: Is it standard practice -- I think it may already be clear, but is it standard practice to always take two views of any fracture?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes. It's absolutely standard practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the 1992 X-rays that you have, that you examined, did you have two views in that case?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the 2001 X-rays, did you have two views in that case?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the 1992 X-rays, did they conform to the standard protocol for how X-rays were taken -- should be taken?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in 2001?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Domazet asked you that in the example that Dr. Vucetic talked about, there was a fracture of the fibula apparent in one but not in the other. And he -- and your answer was, in general, it is possible, but not in this case. Would you please elucidate on that answer?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, the question he asked was is it possible and/or likely that as the example that was apparently shown that you may see no fracture on one radiograph, but if you look carefully at the second one, then you do see the fracture, and yes, that's one of the reasons why we take two X-rays at right angles to one another. But I had both X-rays, and there is no fracture on either of them. So in this case, that comment or question doesn't really apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Doctor, I wonder if you could just clear something up for me? I'm not sure that I fully followed what you had said. You told us, as I recall, that the fracture is likely to have healed after about six months. Now, is there -- is it possible for there to be a refracture, rather than a fresh fracture, as long as about 12 months after the original fracture?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Well, yes. If the patient sustains another injury, they could refracture through the original fracture site, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So the fact that it's healed doesn't prevent it from refracturing? It remains vulnerable to an identical fracture?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: Potentially, yes. It's unusual but it is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And if there is a new incident which places pressure upon where the old fracture was, is it likely to fracture in the same pattern, in the same attitude, et cetera, because of a weakness in the bone?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: If a fracture was to occur at the original fracture site, it would follow the original fracture. I think I tried to say earlier on, if you sustain a second injury, either that will occur or you would get a second fracture at some distance away from the original fracture. What will not occur is what is being suggested here, is that you would have a second fracture close to but not following the original pattern of the first fracture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And you said, as I recall, that you can see only one fracture on the X-rays?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The original -- any of these X-rays?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And that means that either there was no second injury, or if there was, it was a pure refracture of the original injury?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What is the prospects of that happening, say, 12 months after the event?

utterances.speaker: NIGEL RABY
utterances.text: The chances are small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you want to ask any questions about that, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. It's better not, I think, for me to ask any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, very much for coming along to give evidence and the evidence you've given, and you are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you say we're going to have some process by which these PowerPoint demonstrations are preserved?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Once the doctor has an opportunity to take his equipment out, we will bring him down to our computer lab, where he will print out or get us some kind of copy of everything we've seen today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the next expert has to set up his equipment, which also includes some kind of audiolink so that we can hear the speech. This took about 15 minutes to set up this morning. I would anticipate with the audiolink at least 20 minutes to set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: First of all, this has to be dismantled --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- and then the next one has to be put in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So how long do you think? It's not worth waiting around to start before lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That would be my suggestion, Your Honour, we start first thing this afternoon with the Professor. I don't believe he's going to be very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Is he the only other witness we've got today?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. May I ask, Mr. Domazet, bearing in mind the leave we've granted for you to call evidence, to reopen your case as well, have you been able to make any arrangements for the witnesses to be given visas, et cetera, bearing in mind the troubles we've had before?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I have been informed by the Witness and Victims Unit, there will be no problems with the visa and his travel, but as we said before, there was no need for this witness to come in view of the fact that you, too, were of the opinion that this witness should not be recalled. If necessary, the Witness and Victims Unit can organise his travel, and they said they could do that already on Saturday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't know whether we're talking about the same witness. If you remember, when Mr. Groome sought to call Witness VG117 in reply and we indicated fairly clearly that we didn't think it was an appropriate matter in reply after you had objected to it, there was then some discussion about having the Prosecution case reopened, and you said that you had witnesses that you would have called from the school to demonstrate that the person there who was purporting to be from the Red Cross was somebody, not the accused, but who resembled him. Now, I'm worried about you calling that witness or those witnesses. Have you been able to talk to the Victims and Witnesses Section about them?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I had someone else in mind. I was thinking of the other person that we agreed should not come to testify. As for this witness, let me tell you that talking to Mr. Vasiljevic now, discovered that there was a person but whose name we don't really know. We just know the name of a relative. And now we would have to look for that person. We still have to establish the identity of that person, because that really was not part of my case in the pre-trial brief, because the event in the Vuk Karadzic School and the women brought from Velika Gostulja on the 22nd of June were events that were not considered at all. And in fact, this morning I heard that the Prosecution had that evidence at the time but didn't want to use it. They didn't want to call that witness. I have never received the statement of VG117 in the disclosure process, and even now we don't really have a statement. So I was really not in a position to verify any of that. I will do my best to react very quickly, but I fear that the position I am in gives me very little time. I will do my best to do something during the weekend, but to be quite frank, it will be extremely difficult, especially as I still don't have the statement of that lady, nor her testimony. So as for the people who were working there, if that was the Red Cross at all that was listing the people in that school, because this was something I did not investigate at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand the difficulties that you will have, and we'll certainly allow you to do what is necessary to follow it up. I'm a little worried when you say you heard this morning that the Prosecution had the evidence but had decided not to use it, because that is exactly what was said yesterday by Mr. Groome, and we asked him to explain why he hadn't called this witness in his case in chief. It's not something we found out anyway other than what we've been told in court. But I have been shown a document which is a little bit more extensive than was in that list of witnesses. Have you given that to Mr. Domazet, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was no statement taken in this case. There were some investigator's notes. They were provided to Mr. Domazet on Wednesday regarding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That, I think, is the document we have, about a three-page document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. You have nothing better than that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No. But it's perhaps not the best, but it certainly does demonstrate the nature of the evidence she can give. But I do emphasise what I said this morning. She's not going to be allowed to give evidence about other matters than the one very limited issue upon which you've been given leave to reopen your case. And it really is a simple, straightforward matter once you look at it from that point of view. She saw somebody she says was the accused and that he said that he was from the Red Cross and that was going to help them in some way in being relocated. That's so, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That would be the entire substance of her testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Domazet, we will understand if you can't produce somebody next week about it, but I don't want this to go on too long. As you can see, there's a very real problem about running two trials in tandem with two judges sitting something like nine or ten hours a day. So I want to get everything that we can get done by the end of next week before the end of next week. It clearly will not be the addresses, you will be very grateful to hear because you will not have to spend this weekend preparing an address, but nevertheless, anything to do with evidence I would expect to be given as soon as possible, hopefully next week. But if you can't, then that's too bad. We've just got to allow you the time. Is there something you want to add, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not on this matter, Your Honour, but on another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there anything else you want to put, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, I will try and see what I can do, because it is in the interest of the Defence to produce such evidence if accessible. As for the closing address, I am appreciative of all the problems the Chamber has, but I would request, even if we do complete the case by the end of next week, that we are given sufficient time for our written submissions, because the preparation of the closing address itself will take one day or less than one day, as far as I have been able to gather from Mr. Groome. So could that day be fixed at a later date, when the other members of the Trial Chamber would be free. So we would come just for that closing address. And so that would give me time to prepare my closing address at home in my own office, where I have much better facilities than I do here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I have already accepted that you won't be able to give us an address by the end of next week, and certainly now that we are going to have a break, it would be preferable that your written final brief was complete rather than having to add to it as we had originally suggested in relation to the evidence given this year. We also understand, or at least certainly as an old advocate I can understand that the case has swivelled in many ways, even over the last two days, that you will have to treat with some care in your final addresses, and for that reason alone it would be better to have everything we can from you in writing. What -- if we can finish the evidence, except perhaps for this one witness of yours, and provided that your cross-examination of the Prosecution witness doesn't open up a Pandora's box, the best thing to do would be to fix a date a few weeks down the line to enable this other trial to get well under way and then we could perhaps have each of you on separate days so it's not a full four-hour, four-and-a-half-hour day. That would break it up for the Judges who have to sit on two trials at once. But we worry about the particular time that you need for your final addresses when we know when the evidence is going to finish. So I don't think there's any point in trying to fix that now, but you may be assured that you will be given the opportunity to put in final written briefs after the evidence has finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, Mr. Groome. You had some other matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This is a matter I meant to raise on Wednesday. I just keep forgetting it. Over the Christmas break, the Prosecution had D26 examined by forensic experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: D26. It's the ledger from Visegrad hospital covering the time period that includes the 14th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We have the results of that. I want to -- I've made Mr. Domazet aware of the results. It's perhaps something that we can put into evidence in agreement. utterances.text: Mr. Broeders, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us shortly your professional background in forensic speech and audio analysis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Name and address would be -- at least the name might help. His name first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Ton Broeders. I've been working for the Dutch Forensic Science Institute since 1988, and I've worked in the field of speech and audio analysis since I joined. I've been involved in case work ever since I joined the institute in 1988 virtually, and I've -- in the course of these years, I've joined and also been a founding member of an organisation which is active in this area. The organisation is called the International Association for Forensic Phonetics. I'm presently a member of the Executive Board of this organisation. utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Mr. Broeders, last August did you receive from the OTP a minicassette and a normal cassette in your laboratory?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Broeders, what were the principal exercises you undertook with these tapes?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated in my report, I was originally first asked to improve the intelligibility of the recording, to do an enhancement job so to speak. Later, I was also asked to compare -- to compare the voice of a male speaker in a particular part of this recording on the microcassette with material -- with reference material of a known speaker, so that was what I was asked to do at a later stage, and that is also when the minicassettes which I refer to on page 2 of my report were submitted to me. So that was in August, at the end of August, of last year.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Broeders.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have here a pseudonym sheet in case it becomes important to refer to names, that those names are not referred to, and I would just hand it out to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, it will become an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: It's P93.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: P93. That will be Exhibit P93, and is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: So Mr. Broeders, in case you have to refer to the names, please use the pseudonyms that are attributed to those two names. Now, Mr. Broeders, what are the two methods you used to -- in order to compare the voices or make a speech analysis?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: What I did was I used the method that I normally use in this type of examination, which, in fact, is also explained to some extent in the appendix to the report which I've submitted. And the examination actually consists of two parts. One part is basically an auditory analysis of the material, and the second part is an acoustic analysis of the material. So that is what I did. What I think is special in this case is that as far as the auditory analysis is concerned, an important element of the auditory analysis would also be a linguistic and phonetic analysis of the material. Because the material in question concerns a language that I'm not expert of, or even that I even speak myself, in these cases what I will tend to do, what I will always do, is to find somebody who is suitably qualified to do a linguistic or phonetic analysis, and preferably both, so that is what has happened in this case too. So those parts of the analysis that I cannot perform myself because of this limitation in my knowledge in the cases of languages that I am not familiar with, those elements of the analysis have been done by somebody else. This is also indicated in my report, and the specific findings of this native speaker expert have also been set down on paper and are, I think, an enclosure of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I wonder, Ms. Bauer, whether we could have some definition given to us of linguistic and phonetic analyses, because I have a feeling that this witness may have a different view to the Defence witnesses' views.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would be happy to try and do that. A linguistic analysis is one where essentially what you try to do is describe in as much detail as possible the language variety which is used. To refer to English as an example, because that is perhaps one that some of us are familiar with, it is clear that one can distinguish various varieties of English, which to some extent will be regionally marked but they might also be socially marked. In other words, there are a number of parameters in terms of which a language variety can be described. When it comes to the pronunciation level of the variety, then we speak of a phonetic analysis, so then we are going to be looking in depth, if you like, in detail, at the accent, the style of pronunciation, the style of speech that is used. So that is what would happen in a speaker identification examination. An analysis would be made of the unknown material and also an analysis would be made of the reference material, and of course, in order for there to be support for identity, you would expect those analyses to correspond to some extent. To the extent to which they disagree would be an indication of non-identity, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Broeders, after you did your acoustic analysis which you were able to do on your own, what were the preliminary findings you had?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: The preliminary findings were that what is important as part of the preliminary findings is the quality of the materials that were submitted. The questioned material is of poor quality in this sense, that the speakers are removed considerably from the microphone, as a result of which the sound quality or the recording quality of the speech is not very good. In photographic terms, you could say that the resolution is not very high, if that helps, that metaphor. So part of the initial, the introductory, examination is always to assess the quality and the suitability of the material for the examination. So that has also happened here. So as I've already said, the questioned material is -- possibly it was recorded surreptitiously, I don't know, but anyway, it sounds very much as though the speakers were quite removed -- some distance removed from the microphone. The reference material also had important limitations in that although it was plentiful in terms of quantity, I mean there is a lot of it in terms of duration, they were recorded in conditions with a lot of reverberation, which in itself is not ideal but also it differs very clearly from the questioned material. And the importance of the seriousness of this difference in recording conditions can be illustrated perhaps by telling you that there are automatic speaker identification procedures, but these are very, very sensitive to differences in recording conditions. Now, perhaps that helps to understand it also when you apply method which depends heavily on auditory analysis, that differences in recording conditions are also very, very awkward and can make it much more difficult to make an examination than if the conditions are ideal or more suited to the examination. So that was also part of the initial conclusions, that the material did not allow, in the positive sense anyway, a very strong conclusion. Let me perhaps explain. It is sometimes easier to draw a negative conclusion than it is to draw a positive conclusion. So you do not always have to have hi-fi quality material in order to draw a negative conclusion, a conclusion of non-identity.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, was the -- but the quality of the questioned material, was it good enough to make any comparison or was -- would you have said it was -- is your conclusion that it was difficult to make an analysis but it wasn't impossible?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: It is definitely the latter, so it was difficult but it was not impossible. If I'd felt it was impossible, my judgement would eventually have been -- my conclusion would have been no judgement, because that is also one of the ways in which an examination can be concluded. So that is one of the first decisions you have to make, and that is, you know, is the material -- does it lend itself to the examination at all? And it does with the limitations that I've tried to explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And the questioned material, what were sort of the conclusions at first? Was it -- the questioned materials, was it one conversation? Was it -- was there any evidence of -- that this particular sequence of the conversation was altered in any way?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, what -- what happened, of course, was that initially I was asked to concentrate on part of a recording on a particular side of a microcassette, so to give you the full picture, as it were. So I did not necessarily look in detail at the entire recordings of the entire microcassette. There are two sides, and there are signals, there are recordings on both sides. But the interest of the Prosecution clearly was on a particular excerpt on side A, I think. So that is what I concentrated on. I did look at the rest of the contents of the tape also but not in as much detail as you would wish to do if you were going to do a full-fledged integrity examination. However, for the passage of interest, I did look in very considerable detail to see if this contained any indications of any discontinuities which may occur in a recording, and in fact, I did find one discontinuity which obviously, you know, I tried to account for in a sense that as the question was aiming at: Is there any evidence of discontinuity? Is there any evidence of the tape having been manipulated? Well, an important point to make first perhaps is that when the cassette came to my laboratory, the safety tab had not been removed. So that means that if it was put into a tape recorder at any stage, it might have been -- the recording might have been over-recorded, if you see what I mean. So that is the first routine check that we do. So we remove the safety tab so that we ourselves could not make an accidental over-recording. So that means that, theoretically anyway, it could easily have become subject to over-recording, involuntary over-recording even. I'm not saying it has been, I'm just saying that, you know, theoretically the safety tab hadn't been removed which perhaps should have been done. In the passage in question, I did find one discontinuity, and I would happy to show it to the Court if I may. I don't know if that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, but I wonder if you could just explain, at least to me, when you say "discontinuity," is it simply a break in the recording, that recording has been turned off and on again, or is there some interference apparent in the tape itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm using the term "discontinuity" advisedly, I hope, in the sense that I wish to avoid implying any causes or implying, you know, how it arose. So I'm taking a very sort -- I'm trying to take a very careful, cautious position where I say I'm looking for discontinuities. I'm not jumping to conclusions as to why they arose. And that is always a separate issue anyway, I think personally, you know, what the explanation for it is. I can show you what I found and perhaps that will help clarify the issue. I don't know if you can see this at all on your screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is it on the computer or the video?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: It is on computer. However I would like also, in order that everybody can follow better, I mean, we can show it, but also that Mr. Broeders is marking the English transcript where he detected this slight interruption of the transcript of this recording, and it's Exhibit 109.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That can be shown on the ELMO there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Do you have a copy?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yeah. I think so, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: So there's a line between 15 and 16 in the text, and that is exactly where the discontinuity occurs. So after the original text in B/C/S where it says: "... she fell over him," and then just before the question: "On 27th June," there is this discontinuity which I can show on the screen, on the computer, and I can actually play this part of the passage. I can first point it out. If you can see my -- the arrow on your screens, this is where it is, okay? And this is where the woman's voice, the woman says, "27th June," and this is the answer, I think, by the male voice. Let's just go through this passage so that you can hear the right passage, I hope.

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Okay. So this is the discontinuity. This is the question, and this is the answer, I think. So once more.

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: So that is the -- in the excerpts that I was asked to concentrate on, this is the only discontinuity I have found. Now, I'd like to clarify this a little bit, and that is that unfortunately, perhaps, in this day and age, it is possible -- I'm not saying it has happened, far from it, but it is possible to -- to enter a recording into a computer system and to permutate it, to change it, to alter it, to edit it in such a way that technically, technically it is not detectable if it's done properly and if it's done competently. So in other words, it is the fact that you do not find traces of interference in a tape recording on a cassette or whatever doesn't necessarily mean it hasn't taken place, unfortunately, because as I said, in a computer system there is software, which is not even very expensive, which can be -- which in fact I have on this laptop, that can be used to cut and paste, in popular terms, in such a way that technically it's not possible. So I have to make that reservation. What we have here is in fact a -- is in fact a discontinuity which I think personally I cannot fully account for. I cannot be sure it is not what -- it is not what an over-recording would look like, and I would like to show you what that looks like perhaps. I hope I'm making myself clear when I use the term "over-recording." The term "over-recording" I use to indicate that suppose you have a recording which has a certain duration. If you put that cassette into a recorder and you press the record button, then you make an over-recording of an existing recording. That is not normally what you want to do, obviously. That is what I call an over-recording, making a recording on top of another recording. If you do that, you will normally always leave a smoking-gun-type signal, and I can show you that because it occurs -- I think it occurs on -- at one stage on this recording. After seven minutes of this recording, we have a brief passage where I think it occurs. I'm trying to find the exact coordinates now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Mr. Broeders, just to clarify, if you say "recording," do you talk about the recording as such, the whole tape, or do you speak about the sequence we are concerned with --

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: I'm now --

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: -- on my question --

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: I'm now -- I'm now outside the sequence that we are concerned with. So the example I'm hoping to give is one which occurs in -- at seven minutes from the beginning of the tape, and our sequence, if you like, is at roughly 20 minutes after the beginning of the tape. But I'm just mentioning it to illustrate, I hope, what I mean -- what a recording -- over-recording looks like, and -- sorry. I'm just trying to find the position. I have to have the list for that. I'm sorry. Got it. 7:44 is the time. So here we have a passage which sounds like this:

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: And what this looks like to me is you have a similar discontinuity that I was showing earlier, and this may have arisen because somebody was listening to the tape and was accidentally briefly touching the record button. In my experience, in those cases where I've done these types of examinations, I've actually quite regularly come across recordings where, for example, policemen, in listening to a recording, accidentally pressed the record button and created an over-recording, you know, where that was the explanation for that occurring. So what is different from what I've just showed you in the relevant excerpt is that here we have clearly this sequence of events, you know, which is considerably longer. So it does not look like an over-recording. That is the point that I'm trying to make. I cannot fully account for it, but it doesn't look like an over-recording.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Broeders, if we go back to the transcript and look at the transcript, the portion of the questioned material above this interruption is completely -- is one sequence with no signs of any interference, interruption, or alteration?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: That's right. So the only place within the excerpt of interest, if you like, is -- is the one that I've just mentioned. Before that there is nothing. After that, also, there is nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Did you find a similar interruption at the rest of the tape, not any more in the sequence but in the rest of the tape, as you found in this particular portion?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes. There is one that I found at -- sorry, at 23 -- well, right at the beginning of the tape, I also found one or two which look similar, and I think these may be accounted for as false starts. It's very often the case, if you get recordings that are made by civilians, not professional recordings made by policemen or professional recordings in the recording industry but recordings made by individuals, private individuals, that the tapes tend to get a little bit messy because they check first whether the recording works, et cetera, so it's -- that is always difficult, or it may be very difficult to reconstruct exactly what has happened. And in those very early stages of the tape, there are one or two things that might point to recordings, beginnings of recordings.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Is there any other plausible explanation apart from that somebody accidentally pressing an erase head or a recording button that you would take into account that could have happened?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: The problem with microcassette recorders - and there is every reason to believe that this recording was made with a microcassette recorder - is that they tend to be relatively cheap and also not relatively high quality and they tend to -- they may malfunction. The discontinuity may have arisen as a result of some sort of temporary hiccup in the tape transport, but that is a speculation on my part. It is not unusual for things to occur, events to occur, in this type of recording equipment that one cannot immediately account for, precisely because the equipment is relatively cheap. And it is also, for example, difficult to reproduce switching transients which one uses to examine tapes, because usually you rely on switching transients to be consistent and to be the same whenever you make certain action, but on very cheap equipment, there is not the consistency that you would ideally expect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you mean by that expression "switching transients"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A switching transient is an event that takes place and that is visible and audible very often when, for example, a recording stops. I can show you one because on this tape, you can see here, for example, there is an interruption in the recording and there is one here. Now, at the end of this recording, if I can zoom in, you can see, I hope, a switching transient, if I zoom in a little bit more, and here you are. So this is the recording and this is where it ends, and this may together constitute a switching transient. Perhaps a slightly better example is at 2534. That's a little bit -- 2534, zoom out a little bit. Almost there. So this is a better example, actually, of what I mean. So this is the end of the recording and this is a typical -- this is what you typically expect to see when you switch off and end the recording. This is -- there are two heads in a tape recorder, a record head and an erase head, and what happens typically is the tape first passes the erase head, the erase head erases the tape, and then the tape that has been erased goes through the record head. Now, what you see is when you switch off, when you stop the recording, both these heads will leave a mark and those marks are visible on the tape, on the recording. So those are switching transients. And what I'm saying is that these are consistent in good quality equipment but in bad quality equipment, unfortunately, they are not always consistent. They are not always the same, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: So doctor, from all the analyses you conducted, did you find any obvious signs of alteration or possible intervention with this tape?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: I found no signs, no indications of positive interference with the tape, except the one at seven minutes that I mentioned and the one at 23 minutes in the excerpt of interest, which we have talked about, which I've tried to say what I think about. So in other words, there are no indications that the tape has been tampered with, but I have to make the proviso that I made earlier, that it is theoretically always possible for a tape to have been tampered with in such a way that technically there are no traces left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I just ask you this? The blip that we had in the passage of interest, as you call it, when I asked you whether that was interfering with the tape or just interfering with the operation of the tape, you said that you were being very careful to use non-judgemental descriptions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you had to find out which it was, what do you have to do, and did you do it here and, if so, what result did you get?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think if -- what I'm trying to say is that basically, a technical examination will only tell you in the best case, if you're lucky, what has factually happened, whether there was any bona fide or mala fide attitude on the part of whoever did it is difficult to say. That is, a technical examination will not normally tell you that. And what I would rather say is that if there is a -- some sort of technical intervention in the tape, then I think it is also, for a non-technical person, possible to determine what the likelihood is of this being a bona fide or a mala fide action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you able to say, for example, that it was the original tape, that it hasn't been copied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a very interesting and very difficult question, because then we are going into the field of authenticity: Is this the original tape? The only way really -- this question has come up in this same Tribunal in an earlier case, that I'm aware of, perhaps even more. The problem with that is that you need a claim -- in order to usefully examine that question, you need a claim from somebody that it is an original tape, okay? So if somebody says it's a copy, then that's the end of the route technically speaking. That's the end of the route. A copy cannot be authenticated. But if you have a story, a sort of chain-of-custody story, then you can check that story and you can check the tape against the story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But is there any way of telling from the tape itself that it has been copied itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not -- there are circumstances when it's not possible because -- I can give you an example. If you have a recording in your computer, if you digitise a recording, then you can copy that on to a cassette and you can do that in such a way that you do not have any switching transients except at the end, which will only tell you it was made on that tape recorder, which is, you know, fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So there is no way of telling from the tape itself whether it's a copy or an original?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There may be indications, but what I'm trying to say is if there are no indications, even then you can't be sure. There may be very obvious indications that there are over-recordings, for example, in a tape, and then you know that something is missing, okay? But it is -- but if you do not find an indication, then you cannot conclude from that so it must be a virgin, authentic tape, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Bauer, but I thought that the witness had got to the stage where I had to know that. You proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Doctor, after you compared -- you applied this technical method and you inquired with a linguist from the linguistic point of view, what would you say were the overriding conclusions that you came to?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, given the quality of the questioned material and also the quality of the reference material and the misfit, to some extent, in terms of both the recording conditions and also the communicative context, a term which I use to indicate the context in which the language is used -- after all, what happens is that the questioned material is what sounds like a very informal gathering of a number of people with a recording which may, in fact, have been made surreptitiously. The reference material is a relatively formal situation where there is an interrogator or an interviewer from the Tribunal who is talking to somebody, to the reference speaker. These are very different circumstances, and you have to allow for differences to arise simply because the communicative context, the context in which the speakers were engaged, is very different. Speech has a very important behavioural aspect, dimension, and the behavioural dimension will vary with the situation in which a speaker finds himself, more so for some speakers than for others, but there is this possibility. So there is a certain amount of difference can be -- is -- can be accounted for. For example, if the language is much more informal in one context than another, then maybe that is not necessarily an indication of non-identity. That may be accounted for by the difference in context. So bearing these different technical and communicative considerations in mind, then the conclusion was that there is a considerable degree of similarity. Also, apparently, in terms of the linguistic and phonetic analysis that was performed by the expert native speaker, but at the same time, the quality of the material is such that you have to allow for the possibility that if you were going to compare a lot of -- a relatively large number of speakers with this questioned material, that once or twice, you might come across a similar degree of similarity, a similar degree of correspondence. That's what I'm trying to say in my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: If you say a relative large numbers of speakers, do you mean any speaker or a speaker of a confined area?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, yes. Well, I was going to say obviously, but apparently it's not obvious. I would be assuming clearly the linguistic analysis makes it clear that for anybody to qualify as the questioned speaker, they would have to meet those requirements, in other words they would have to be speakers of that particular variety. Okay? So that by itself reduces the number, so we are not talking about the western hemisphere in terms of male speakers. We are talking about somebody who would meet linguistic profile, so who would come from the area that the linguistic profile indicates roughly. He might not live there but linguistically speaking. So I'm talking not -- I mean, you know, it's difficult to put a figure there, but I'm saying a relatively large number of people and that means not if you take ten, you're likely to find somebody who is equally similar, but I am thinking of hundreds or thousands. That's what I'm thinking of.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Broeders, you also had an opportunity to look at Defence witness's' report on the subject. My first question would be, from the face of the report, did you have any indication that this person is an expert in the sense of forensic audio and speech analysis?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, that's a question you can answer in several ways. One way of answering it is that I -- because of my -- partly because of my functions, I mean, you know, my position, in the international speech and audio -- forensic speech and audio analysis context, I have never come across this person's name. So that is an indication. But apart from that, if I look at the report itself, what strikes me is that Professor Krstic calls himself criminalist, which is obviously a very wide field, and I think at the -- on the final page of the report, he also adds criminology or professor of criminology, which is an entirely different -- well, not entirely, but it is a different field again. The other thing that strikes me about the report is perhaps it strikes me more in what it fails to do than in what it does do. What it fails to do is it does not address the report proffered by the Prosecution. More specifically, in the Prosecution report there is a linguistic, a phonetic analysis of the language variety of the questioned material and the reference material. I have not found hardly -- I found hardly any references to that, to the Prosecution report. And also, I have not found a counter or alternative analysis or any argument about the analysis except for one -- one passage in the report, which is the one about the vocals of Serbian, which I'm afraid I am at a loss to fully understand. That is something that happened to me a number of times, I have to say, that in some -- in places, the report was not terribly clear to me. In some cases, because I know the field relatively well, I was able to infer sometimes what was meant. But to come back to my point, it is particularly striking, I think in -- that it does not address the main issue, in the sense that it does not offer an analysis of the material at issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now, doctor, as you said, there were four parts mainly to this report, and one of it was, in the beginning, a psychological analysis of the speech, I believe. Is this a method you would apply as --

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: -- phonetic?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: -- the -- after an introduction which touches on a number of general issues which are interesting but, I mean, do not really address the main issue, there is a section on -- which is called a psychological analysis. Now, I, as a linguist and a phonetician, as a member of the organisations that I have mentioned, I would not embark on such an exercise myself, nor would any of my colleagues. In fact, the IFP, the International Association for Forensic Phonetics, has a code of practice and the code of practice explicitly tells members of the organisation not to engage in psychological profiling, not to engage in statements about the truthfulness of speech recordings that are submitted for examination. That is not to say that, forensically speaking, these are completely irresponsible activities. The issue, of course, of psychological profiling is a very important one, but I think it should be addressed by psychologists, and it should not be addressed by linguists or phoneticians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Broeders, do you know this International Association of Voice Identification to which Professor Krstic belongs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know the organisation. You may have seen -- I've also added the Interpol review that I wrote for the triennial Interpol forensic science symposium. What -- I try to do that and the reason I've added it is because it gives my idea of the present state of the art in the field. I also refer to the organisation except that I call it by slightly different name. On page 5 of 22 of this report, the Interpol report, I refer to the International Association for Identification, IAI, which has a subcommittee, the VIAAS, which in fact is a group of people who work in modified tradition of the voiceprint. Now, the voiceprint technique is extremely controversial and was subject to a fairly strong condemnation or a very critical study undertaken by Bolt and others in the 1970s, I think it was, or 1968. All of these matters I refer to in my Interpol report. And I think I would take issue with the suggestion made by Professor Krstic that the most advanced state of the art in terms of speaker identification is to be found in the United States. In fact, the actual state of affairs in the United States is, as I have described it in my Interpol report -- Michael Saks, who is a very prominent professor, American professor of law and psychology, has made a survey into the extent to which speaker identification is accepted by American courts, and in America, in the United States, the experts, most of them, are working in the IAVI and the admissibility of that type of evidence by these practitioners is limited to say -- to -- you know, to qualify it. So I know the organisation. I know that it is a group of people who have evolved out of using voiceprints. Some of the members of the organisation are excellent phoneticians. Peter Ladefoged is one, is a phonetician, Professor of Phonetics in the University of California, Los Angeles. He's mentioned also by Professor Krstic. And I can only say that Peter Ladefoged is one of the most prominent phoneticians around. So it's not -- I'm not saying that the organisation that you refer to doesn't have very good phonetician members.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Broeders, Professor Krstic, in his report, does he view as the voiceprint actually the form of speaker identification as a valid and a good form of speaker identification?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, I must say that a lot of time reading through Professor Krstic's report, I agree entirely with a lot of what he says. So -- I mean, some bits of the report I like very much because I agree entirely with them; other bits I find difficult to understand. But I agree, I think, with Professor Krstic where he condemns the voiceprint approach, which I think he is doing. What I have a little -- what I have problems with, in fact, is his conclusion.
