The conclusion of his report, at the very end is one that puzzles me considerably, because although the actual content of it I -- you know, is perhaps not very difficult, the argument that he uses I find very puzzling. Because on page 23 of his report, and that's the final page that I have, it says "Opinion," and then in the last -- very last sentence it says: "Since in the delivered material for which it is claimed that it originates from the same speaker, there are no identical characteristics of the voiceprint," and this puzzles me, because to the extent that I understand his argument, he does not approve of using voiceprints. He disapproves strongly and yet it is used as an argument on which the conclusion is based, and I find that not comprehensible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you again? I'm sorry. Mr. Domazet, we have not got Professor Krstic's CV yet, have we? You said that was being translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will receive the CV in English. I may have it ready this evening, but I'm sorry, I don't have it on me right now, because I think it is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I was looking for it, and I'm glad to say it isn't because I've lost it. I just haven't been given it yet. I'm sorry to have interrupted you, but I just thought it might help, because I remember asking whether this particular person was a psychiatrist. Yes. Well, you proceed, Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Another criteria or subject of Professor Krstic's report is the influence of a so-called cocktail party phenomena on the examination. Would you see that as a very crucial point in this -- in these circumstances we are talking about here?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, the cocktail party effect is a well-known concept in auditory phonetics, in the study of the perception of speech, and it is used to refer to the, in a way, surprising ability of human beings to concentrate on one voice in the middle of a cacophony of voices, in the middle of a multitude of voices. That is something that human beings can do. We can follow, we can hook on to a speaker even when there are lots of people speaking at the same time. The relevance of that effect to this particular recording is not entirely clear to me because in the relevant passage anyway, the passage of interest, most of the time the speakers are taking turns. So there is no question of picking one voice out of a lot of voices. The speaker -- the woman asks questions sometimes and the man answers it or he volunteers. He tells a story. But there is no simultaneous speech from, you know, an X number of speakers. So to that extent I'm not sure what the relevance of the cocktail party effect is to the taped material that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: As the third part, Professor Krstic sort of had a chapter on characterisation of vocals in Serbian language. I think we are not quite sure what he meant with vocals, but what was your conclusion on that section of his report?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: That is in fact a section that I find difficult to follow, I hope not because of a lack of knowledge on my part, although that is always possible. I think what -- this is the one area where I think he does actually come to a statement which could be part of a linguistic profile in the sense that if I understand it correctly, he says that the voice is undisputed Serbian. Now, again, you know, we get into a very difficult area of what is a language. What is a dialect? How many dialects are there? Let me say that from a linguistic point of view, there is no way, from a linguistic point of view, that you can define a language or a dialect. The best answer to that question that was given by a very prominent linguist - whose name I forget - is that a language is a dialect with an army and a navy. So in other words, the question of a particular language variety is a language or a dialect political one. It is not a linguistic one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But, Doctor, may I give you an example where I think that could not be so? Coming home on the tram last night, I was sitting in front of two people who were clearly from the Office of the Prosecutor and who did not realise that they had an English speaker sitting in front of them, and they were chatting. Now, as an Australian - I am - I was able to determine quite clearly that the male was a New Zealander, and I did so because of the vowels.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Fulp" [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, there are some other words that you could use that are well-known to demonstrate the problems that New Zealanders have with vowels. Now, that is a dialect, I suppose, of English and New Zealand, just as Australian is. And I was able to determine he was a New Zealander, and I thought probably from the South Island, simply because of the vowels that he used. Is that not a genuinely effective way of determining where a person comes from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. I'm not -- I would hate to suggest that that is impossible. That is very well possible, Your Honour, but the point that I'm trying to make is that where -- I mean, even -- there is ultimately no such thing as New Zealand English because there are always people who are more central, more core New Zealand speakers than others. In other words, at the edges. I mean, it's like the definitions of any concepts. The closer you look at them, the more they evaporate, okay? Now, the point I was trying to make is whether you call something a language or dialect is a political question. The fact that southern British English has become the prestige variety in England is a political accident. If another King had been killed at the right or the wrong time, another variety of English, perhaps Scottish, would have been the prestige variance, okay? So what I'm trying to say is we can distinguish variance of languages wherever we are, but to rate them in a hierarchy as language versus dialect, that is a political question. That's what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But all that Professor Krstic seems to be saying is that the particular person involved here, who has a pseudonym VGD30, came from Serbia or some area of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know if that's what he's saying. What I can read is that his voice is undisputed Serbian. But if I don't know what is understood by "Serbian," it is theoretically possible that Professor Krstic or anybody else calls anything Serbian that he wishes to call Serbian. It's not for me. I mean, it's not -- I mean, the text is unclear in that sense. But you may be right. It is definitely possible to read that into it. That is a possible explanation. But I don't find it particularly clear. And the other thing is that I do not find it supported with arguments. It is a claim which may be correct, which may be incorrect, but it would help us to assess it if there were arguments given, which is what happens in the Prosecution report. At least an attempt has been made to do that. So it is -- it has the status of a more or less gratuitous observation which may be correct, but it's difficult to judge. The rest of this section I find irrelevant to the question. In fact, that is also what Professor Krstic is saying. His definition of vocal is completely erroneous and wrong, I'm afraid to say, from a linguistic point of view, which is why I hesitate to accept that he is a linguist, but that is by the way. The experiment that he reports on the top of that -- at the top of the next page is one into what I think is vowel formants, which is a technical story about the spectral composition of vowels, and there have been many attempts to identify speakers, to distinguish speakers in terms of the spectral composition of their vowel sounds. It's one of the things that you can look into. And these spectral composition of vowel sounds is related to the resonating function of the glottal and oral cavity. So the oral cavity functions as a resonating chamber. You can -- as a physicist, you can measure these resonating chambers and then you can -- you end up with certain figures for what are called formants, and that basis of that you can see if you can identify human beings. What he seems to be saying is that this scientist at the Yugoslav National Institute for Security did this study and found that he was unable to do it. Okay, that's possible and that has been done before, and it is a negative result, as far as I can see, as in fact also Professor Krstic says. But the relevance to the issue is not entirely clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: So in order to conclude this section, did you see any -- any -- anything apart from that he criticises the use or the attribution of a nationality to -- to the speaker, VGD30? Is there anything that would be a counter-thesis to the linguistic report?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: I don't think there's any substance -- anything of substance to contradict or to agree with the points made in the Prosecutor's report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now, on the last -- the last portion was entitled "Phonoscopic, Identification of Voice and Possible Detection In View of the Truthfulness of Its Contents." Could you please comment on this section?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes. I've already indicated that in the organisation that I'm a member of, members are not supposed to make any statements about the truthfulness of the speech that they examine. The -- what I also find somewhat peculiar is the use of the term phonoscopics. The term phonoscopy, I also explained that in the survey that I wrote for the Interpol symposium. The term phonoscopy was used and still is used to some extent, especially in Eastern European countries. There's always been a enormous amount of speaker identification work going on behind the Iron Curtain. Partly -- I don't know, but partly this may have been because the standard of proof or of scientific proof was different from what it was in the West. I don't know. But there was a lot of work going on in Eastern Europe, and in fact there's a reference to this sort of thing going on in Solzhenitsyn, the Red Circle. Now, it still is called phonoscopy. The trouble with the word phonoscopy is that it sounds very scientific. I mean, the trouble in the sense that it suggests more than it is. It has a ring which associates it with dactyloscopy, fingerprint -- fingerprinting for identification purposes. But what is puzzling also is that phonoscopy, as it was practised in Eastern European countries to the -- as far as I'm aware, was not about detecting the truth. It was basically trying to establish whether speakers were identical, but not detecting the truth. So the use of the term phonoscopics here is also somewhat peculiar. None of my colleagues would use that word except again people from Lithuania, Estonia perhaps. You know, from the former Eastern Bloc countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Mr. Broeders, in this section, Professor Krstic lists a number of things which ought to be done in order to make a voice identification. I think -- I think you'd agree that most of the things that he listed that ought to be done are correct. However, did you see anywhere that he undertook this exercise he outlined ought to be done?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: That is -- this is one of the areas where I agree entirely in the sense that, for example, on page 20 -- 20 -- the final page, for example, he says that there are all sorts of things that you can do, that is it is possible -- the final paragraph, just above "Opinion" on page 23. It says, "According to everything stated so far, it is quite possible to talk about speaker sociolect and dialect as well as the problem whether the language in question is the person's native language or to what extent is his language influenced by some other language," and he goes on. I agree, but why doesn't he do it? I mean, that is the -- that is a question that inevitably presents itself. If you say, as Dr. Krstic does, that these are the things that one can do in respect of a language sample, why doesn't he go ahead and do it in respect of this -- the material that we are looking at here? That is what I find a little bit strange.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now, going last again to his opinion, we talked already about the conclusion he had, "There are no identical characteristics of the voiceprint," but he continues to say, "There is a grand possibility that it is not the same speaker." What does this tell you? Does he exclude any possibility that it might be the same speaker?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: I'm not sure what he means by "a grand possibility." I find that -- the impression I get is that the text was translated into English, and not always equally felicitously, so I don't know -- I'm not sure whether it means a great possibility or a small possibility. I think actually probably it means a sizeable, a good possibility, in which case basically the conclusion is the same as that of the -- in the Prosecution's report, essentially, namely that there are similarities but, you know, it is difficult to -- I mean, you know, his conclusion is it is possible it's not the same speaker. The argument that he uses in the same sentence I find incomprehensible, as I've already said. "There are no identical characteristics of the voiceprint," that argument used by somebody who has just explained that voiceprints are not reliable, I find incomprehensible, but again it may be a translation problem there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Broeders, the analytical methods you use in order -- or you used in this -- in this case, are they accepted in courts of different countries?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, again, that is a difficult question because there are common-law countries and there are continental-style countries, there are adversarial systems and non-adversarial systems. In the situation in the United States, where we have the Judge who has the gate-keeper function is the one that was described in my Interpol survey. So in other words, in the United States, whenever you have technical or scientific evidence, you have to go -- you may have to go through a Daubert hearing, and I happened to see on the Internet yesterday that in the United States, fingerprint evidence has been rejected for the first time in history in the sense that the fingerprint expert is not allowed now to say that two fingerprints are a match. So to give an idea of what happens in the United States. Now, in the Netherlands - and that's always a source of confusion - we do not have a system of admissibility of evidence. So any type of evidence is admissible, and it is up to the Judge to decide whether he or she thinks it makes any sense. So it's a difficult question to answer. I can say, yes, it's accepted in the Netherlands, in Belgium, et cetera, but that's meaningless because virtually anything is accepted, except that you may get very little speaking time, as it were, because, you know, it doesn't -- but let me put it this way: In the U.K., contrary to what Professor Krstic says -- and this is a point that I'd like to actually explicitly make, because it's very confusing. On page 25 of the -- sorry, 22 in handwriting, page 22 of his report, he has a paragraph starting with, "It is interesting that." And then he talks about what has happened in the United Kingdom. Now, that's very confusing, what he writes here. What happened in the United Kingdom was that in the sixties or in the seventies, there was an organisation called the British Academic -- sorry, the British Association of Academic Phoneticians -- sorry, the British Association for Academic Phoneticians, the BAAP. These people, who worked at universities passed a motion saying that phoneticians should not appear in courts of law to pronounce upon identity, non-identity of speakers. That's what they said. They said this because they felt that a lot of misinformed and badly informed experts were working in the U.K.. They also said this because they believed there was no reliable method. This has since -- now, what Krstic says is that in his final sentence of that paragraph, "The outcome of which is that the phoneticians there managed to prevent the use of phonoscopics as evidence in court." That is not true at all. First of all, it wouldn't be called phonoscopics. But apart from that, Peter French, Dr. Peter French, somebody who appeared again for this Tribunal last year, is somebody who makes a living appearing in British courts, and that wouldn't be possible if it was not accepted, if this type of evidence was not accepted. So there are at least five or six people that I know who, on a very regular basis, make these kinds of -- do this kind of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But Mr. Broeders, in the U.K. I'm sure it must be the same, it doesn't go under the same name, as the American test, but there must be an acceptance by the Judge that the evidence is -- relates to a recognised scientific procedure. Now, if that has been accepted in the U.K., as it appears to have been, has it been accepted elsewhere in the adversarial systems, where you need to pass such a test?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, what has been happening in the U.K. is that he do not have the strict possibility, because of course in the U.S. nine times out of ten there is no Daubert hearing either, but you can always use it as a defence, but in the U.K., as far as I'm aware, the issue is open, so -- I mean, it hasn't been thrown out in that same sense and -- so there is a difference there. And the Defence may -- I mean, what happens more frequently is that you have Pre-Trial Conferences where the experts of the two parties come together and say, "This is what we agree about and this is where we disagree." So that is the way they try to resolve it. But the issue that you're addressing, the scientific status of the evidence -- of the method as such is not approached head-on, if you like. But what I can say about it is that, as I've already indicated, speech has an important behavioural dimension, like, for example, handwriting, which makes it very ill-suited, if you like, for automatic examination, analysis, et cetera, and also, it makes it difficult to, you know, distinguish. There is a great deal of overlap, possibility of overlap, between different speakers. So in other words, the distinguishing power of speaker identification is -- even under the best circumstances, is poorer, is worse, than, for example, fingerprints, again, if fingerprints are -- if not carried out according to the proper protocols. So I mean, in very popular terms, we are not talking DNA here, right? In very, very popular terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now, in order to go back to the reference material, having read the Defence expert's report and having thought about this issue, would this alter in any way your findings that you conclude that it is possible that it is the same speaker in the reference material and in the questioned material?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: No. The report by Dr. Krstic would not change my report at all, on any points.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: So you would reaffirm that?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes, I would, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just before you start, my list was wrong. I had crossed out the wrong number. So this report will be Exhibit P113. Sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Broeders, good afternoon. I will ask you several questions regarding your report. First of all, could you please look at paragraph 5(3) of the your report, that's on page number 4?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Here, in this section, you explained what the tape 1001 consists of, and this is the tape that is at issue here, and if I understood you correctly, you also stated that on page A, there were six separate recordings. Is that true? On side A, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, I don't have -- I don't know off the top of my head, so to speak, but there were a number of separate recordings, definitely. In fact, I have some sort of rough and ready sketch of the contents of side A, which I'm trying to dig out now, which I could perhaps show the Court. It is a little bit rough and ready, but it gives a good idea, I think. So what we have is -- I'm afraid it's Dutch but it says "side A" at the top and it says "side B" a little lower down. And then side A is the side of interest, and -- so side A and side B and then -- and then here, this is the -- again, I would not like to say that this was one continuous recording because I have to allow for the possibility that there is some false starts at the beginning. I did not look into that. I was not asked to do it, so I didn't really systematically look into it, but here there are clear interruptions. Now, I have to warn you, because this is out of scale, if you like, so the 25 minutes look considerably shorter than the one minute here, okay? So it's out of scale. This should be much, much longer, but the times are there, again in a very rough and ready fashion, 25 minutes, one minute. So essentially, what it looks like on side A is a longish recording of approximately 25 minutes, plus a number of very brief ones which I have not particularly paid attention to, except because to look at the switching transients because I wanted to know what they looked like, to confirm that the recording had been made on a microcassette. Did I answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In this drawing of yours, what are these marks towards the end? So are they the interruptions in the last recording and the one before the last, these markings that you put on?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Are you referring to the discontinuities that we talked about?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, is that what it means?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, I can show you perhaps -- can I switch to the computer again? Because that's -- I can in fact easier now. The -- what you see here is -- this is not all of side A because we were running out of space a little bit, and also what happened after this, here where my mouse is, if you can see that, was not of very great interest. There is no recording there, so we stopped there, but this is the 25 minutes, okay? As you can see at the bottom, because it says 24, 25 minutes, okay? And these are the first two separate recordings, if you like. So this corresponds partly to what you -- to the first part of what you just saw in the drawing, but the drawing gives a complete picture for side A. Now the matter of the -- the passage of interest is the one that's marked here with those two little arrows, if you like. So this is the part of interest that we have been talking about. I can zoom into this, if you like, and then press this button then I zoom in. This is where the marks are again? Okay? And this is the "Mitar, like ... Mitar" passage that starts here, so to speak. Now, the discontinuity was at 25 something -- no, 23 -- sorry, I have to look it up again. Sorry about this. If you list them, we can also find them. Was it 2344 I think actually? Here it is. I've got it. So we now -- this is where it is. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. That's on the ELMO. So could you please show on this drawing of yours that's on the ELMO where what you've just shown us on the computer is?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Somewhere here. Oh, sorry. It's -- this is 25. If this is 25, then it's somewhere here. Because it's 23, 23 minutes into the recording on side A.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since we have transcripts of the part of this tape, did you -- in fact transcripts for the whole recorded material, so for the entire side. Did you make those transcripts at all or not?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: No. I did not make any transcripts. The transcripts that I have looked at was in fact limited to that one or two pages, A4 size, and which were the transcripts of the -- what I call the relevant passage. And what I received was both a B/C/S transcript and an English translation. So that's what I've seen. And, of course, I've listened to the tape a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So you were provided only a transcript of one part of the tape; however, you listened to the entire tape?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you observe any other differences in the tape, as far as the intelligibility of what was recorded is concerned? Is there any difference in other parts as compared to this segment that the Prosecution asked you to examine?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, what I can say is that the 25 minutes recording was of a similar quality, in the sense that when people speak with little effort, it is probably extremely difficult or it may be difficult to make out exactly what they are saying. If they raise their voices, which happens from time to time, I think it's probably easier. My yardstick for this is that with the transcript that I had, I was able to follow, if you like, the native, original language that I was listening to, okay? I could recognise the spelling in the original language that I was hearing. So that gives me some idea of the degree of intelligibility, because although I do a lot of this work, day in and day out, it is difficult to determine the intelligibility of a recording in a foreign language, obviously. As to the rest of your question, what about the rest of the tape, I also remember listening to the B side because what I did after -- simply as a professional -- out of professional curiosity, I'm afraid, when I noticed this one hiccup, my tendency is to see if there are any others on an evidential tape simply because you always want to find out. So I listened to the tape, in the sense that I tried to spot any further hiccups or discontinuities or transients of that sort. I did that very quickly, in the sense that that was not explicitly part of what I was asked to do, but I did nevertheless try to do it systematically.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you followed on the transcript only the part of the tape for which the transcript was provided to you but it is a smaller part of the tape; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: No, no, sorry. In that case, I didn't make myself clear. What I did do was listen to all of the tape except that I wasn't listening for what was being said, because that wouldn't make sense to me most of the time, anyway. But I was listening out for events that might be interesting from a technical point of view, from the point of view of how the recording was made, from the point of view especially of are there any major discontinuities that point to over-recordings, is this what looks like continuous recording, these sort of aspects are things -- and again, in order to do this, you always listen to the tape, to the background noise. If there is a change in the background noise, if there is one, that again may be an indication of something untoward having happened to the tape. So there are -- critical listening is very important, a very important step to any form of tape analysis, and you would always want to do that, and major irregularities or potential irregularities would always be noticed ideally any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will have to take the break now, Mr. Domazet. It's 4.00. We will resume again at 4.30. Before I go, we have no transcript of the whole of this tape, but I notice that at the foot of page 4 of Mr. Broader's report, in the last incomplete paragraph on the page, something which I had never been aware of before, where the -- what's his number, VGD30 has identified himself as such. If that is correct, it may be of some significance in the case. See in the second last line on page 4? Anyway, you might like to look at that over the break. We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Broeders, let us resume where we left off half an hour ago. We were talking about your listening to the tape, and my question was whether you listened to the whole tape and used the transcript only for the relevant part. I asked you this because on the basis of my own listening to the tape, and I refer specifically to the first 25 minutes, the conversation of the speakers, for me at least, was absolutely incomprehensible up to this point which is of significance and which, though with difficulty, was intelligible, which leads me to believe that something is wrong, that it's rather strange that only particular part should be much clearer than the 20 minutes that preceded it, during which at least I, as a layman, was unable to understand anything. I don't know whether you were able to follow in a similar fashion in view of the fact that you don't know the language and whether the person who assisted you and who does know the language could help you in that respect.

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes. What I can say is that the -- what we did do was concentrate on the passage of interest, and although I understand that originally there was an interest on the part of the Tribunal to make a full transcript of the tape, or there may have been an interest in the sense that originally the question that was put to me was to enhance the tape, that was not really followed up, for reasons which I have not looked into and do not really concern me or affect me. So although that was the original request, to improve the enhancement of the tape, the intelligibility of the tape, we actually, as a forensic institute, offered the possibility for a Tribunal Prosecution interpreter to come and make a full transcript, and I think that -- I don't know to what extent this has taken place, because on one or two occasions an interpreter has been -- has come to the forensic institute and has listened to the tape, but the arrangement was that the interpreters or the listeners would make their own transcripts and it would not be a forensic institute transcript, if you see what I mean. So that is also why I don't know whether, in fact, a complete transcript was made. I have never seen it. And I've only listened, concentrated on the passage of interest. Now, your position that it is remarkable that only this passage should be intelligible and the rest should be unintelligible, I'm not really in a position to answer that one because, first of all, I'm not a speaker of the language in question; and secondly, I have not really listened to the tape from that perspective. The perspective that I listened to the tape to was to see if there were discontinuities in the recording situation, differences in background noise, those sort of features which might be indicative of manipulation or whatever. I have not found those, but it is not impossible for a recording of this type, which sounds like a surreptitious recording or a recording where the microphone was removed a long way from the speakers for these recordings to contain passages of different degrees of intelligibility. It is quite natural for that to occur because sometimes conversation can liven up and sometimes they can be less interesting. So I'm afraid I cannot really answer your question on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. But as far as I am -- understand you, this was not done by you. The tape of which I received a copy was not enhanced by you, at least this part of it. I know that you focussed on this particular portion and taped it on another tape, but I am talking about the original tape, and it was not done at your institute, if I understand correctly.

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: The enhanced -- the request was made to make an enhancement. What we do regularly, also with Dutch police and Dutch requests of this type, is that we ask the people requesting this to, first of all, tell us how much they have already on paper and then to come to the laboratory and do the work in -- with using our facilities. You see, it is not easy -- I mean, we cannot simply set a number of knobs and switches to improve a tape. It's very much a very special job in the sense that it is difficult to assess the effect of certain types of filtering. So preferably we have the listener, the person who is making the transcript, there, so that he can interact with the technician and say, "Look, this is the best position for this part of the tape." So that is why -- that is what tends to happen, and as I've already I think also made clear in the report, a lot of the work that is called "tape enhancement" goes on for the purposes of cosmetic improvement of tapes because tapes have to be played in courts and there may be unpleasant noises that can easily be removed. But if it's a matter of subliminal or marginal intelligibility, what I've found is that it is extremely important to have a very good listener who speaks that particular language variety very, very well, and then you can still get a lot of words on paper. But when it comes to the question, "Did you do an enhancement job," well, I've already, I think, tried to indicate what has happened. The request was there. We dealt with it by saying, "These are the facilities." On one or two occasions, an interpreter came along, but I've never seen a complete transcript of the recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you are not a speaker of the language, and you have explained the difficulties you had as a result, could you tell me how great is the influence of the person who knew the language and who took part in this over the final conclusion that you've reached in this case? How great was the influence of the assistance he provided?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: The influence is essential, because if the linguistic or phonetic analysis suggests that there are major discrepancies, major differences, between questioned and reference material, then this type of conclusion could not be drawn. So what I've tried to explain in my report is that if you are dealing with a foreign language, it is absolutely essential that there is in linguistic and phonetic analysis of the language variety, if that is not the case, a very strong proviso, a very strong reservation, has to be made if a conclusion is drawn at all because clearly, if -- I mean, this sort of information is so essential that it is not really responsible to draw a conclusion if that type of analysis cannot take place. So in that sense, it is an essential condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But if we have the opinion of such an expert that this is a dialect spoken by people from eastern Bosnia, bearing in mind that in my opinion - and I don't think you would deny it - that that is a dialect spoken by at least hundreds of thousands of people, if that expert is not also a phonetics expert, to what extent, then, was his assistance decisive? To what extent was his influence important for you?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: In the sense -- it's difficult to quantify, but what I've tried to explain is that it is an essential condition. And what in this type of situation I try to do is to -- although I cannot assess the details of the analysis, I can follow the reasoning behind the analysis. So what I try to do is to make sure that the person I consult uses linguistically sound arguments. Whether these arguments are correct, I cannot really ultimately assess, but I can decide whether they are linguistic arguments, in the same way as I can decide that in the report that was submitted by Dr. Krstic, there are no linguistic arguments that are given.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, but my question was preceded by the statement that a large number of people use that dialect. So I don't know how important that would be when a linguistic expert said that those were people from eastern Bosnia. To what extent was -- did that affect the final conclusion regarding the possibility that this was the voice of one and the same man?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, the conclusion is not that it is the voice of one and the same man, so I think we have to try and -- I would like to repeat that that is not in fact the conclusion. What the conclusion is, is that it is possible that it is the same speaker, and there is a very essential difference there. Again, I can say that if the linguistic analysis had been negative, convincingly negative, then that conclusion would not have been drawn, could not have been drawn. So that is where the importance lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. If I understand you properly, a negative linguistic analysis would be that that person is not using a similar dialect. Is that what you mean when you say "a negative linguistic assessment"?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Generally, yes, unless of course there were reasons to explain why, because some people simply speak two, perhaps even more, varieties of language. I mean, these cases do occur, but normally that would be a cause for further questions, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. That was why I said what I said at the beginning, and that is that an extremely large number of people use that dialect, and in my view, this expands the range of people who could have been the speaker. So, though I did not say that you have said that it was one and the same speaker, but you did say that it was a possibility. But allow me now to go on to another question. Or maybe before I do that, let us clear this up. Let us clear up what His Honour Judge Hunt wanted to ask. So will you please look at page 4, and the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When you do so, you must be very careful not to use the person's name, to use the pseudonym that you've got on that sheet there. Whilst the witness is looking for that, Mr. Domazet, your questioning after the adjournment started off with your own personal experience in listening to this tape. I hasten to add, as I'm sure you are aware, that is not evidence, and if you want to go into the witness box to tell us how the tape sounded, you should do so, but not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Have you found this last paragraph? Will you please avoid mentioning the name, as it has the pseudonym VGD30, but the explanation: "Since his voice on Exhibit 2002 is not in dispute, it would follow from this that it is not in dispute on Exhibit 2001 either," which obviously is not the case. So could this be an error in the report itself, a slip?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: That's always possible, I'm afraid, except that I don't quite see it. I was working, apparently, on the assumption that the material that I call 2001 and 2002 was not question material but reference material. Is that a wrong assumption?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It may be that I have led you all into this problem, and I'm sorry if I have done so, but this report came to me only as you came to give evidence, and I read it a little bit too hurriedly. I see on the front page or page 2 of your report you have identified it as the conversation with the investigator. I had misread it, and I am sorry for having done so. I'm afraid, Mr. Domazet, I'm at fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] Very well, then. I withdraw that question, and there's no need for us to go into it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your conclusions which are to be found in paragraph 5.8 and then in paragraph 6, there is an addition by you in which an explanation is given that the name or the shortened name of this person is mentioned in the conversation, and you highlight this as being significant for identifying the speaker. I would agree with you if that man had actually uttered those words and if the whole thing is not planted. So the question is: Could somebody have acted out that part, too, if we can use that term, if everything may have been said by a person who used this name and said what he did without it actually being the witness himself, who is absolutely denying having participated in such a conversation altogether?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes. The reason -- actually, why this was added in the report is that this is what we -- this is normal practice in the reports that I write. Sometimes recorded material contains internal evidence that might point to, point to the identity of the speakers. I would not say it was significant. I would say it might be relevant. That is also the spirit in which I've written it. It is not -- I would hate to suggest that it is conclusive; far from it. It is an indication that ultimately may carry some weight. The least you can say is that it may be relevant, and that is also why it was included. More specifically as to your question whether if you start from the assumption that this whole recording or this part of the recording is a frame, is a put-up job, if you like, well, of course anything is possible from that point of view. It is always possible for that scenario to be the case. So you cannot exclude that possibility at the same time. The real question, I suppose, is how much evidence is there for it, because that ultimately decides the reality value of that scenario.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the very beginning when you were explaining, you told us in a very fair manner and a correct manner all the possibilities for abuse, and you said that it was absolutely possible - I think you used the word "computerised" - for a computerised conversation to be taped over the original tape without one being able to notice it through an expert analysis. Did I understand correctly what you said at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let me also ask you: A witness was heard here in court who said himself that he participated in this conversation, and he said that he -- or, rather, she switched on the tape recorder and later switched it off. She claimed that there were no interruptions and that the conversation was taped for about one hour and a little longer. Would that be possible on the basis of your analysis and your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, I think it's fairly obvious that on side A of this cassette there are interruptions, because if you -- I don't know if you still have this picture in front of you, but there are a number of takes, if you like, a number of separate recordings on side A , but it is not clear to what extent that is necessarily a problem. Whether it can be reconciled with the statement that a recording was made of one hour's duration is a different matter, but then I think we very easily enter into the realm of correct -- the correctness of memories of people, and that is an area in which I am not competent except to say that, you know, the -- what people tend to do when they make a recording is they may well forget about all the false starts that they made. I mean, that is something that people -- because it doesn't appear to be relevant. So for one thing, that is something that you find on a tape. On the other hand, the duration of the recording that looks continuous on side A is 25 minutes, and the other bits are relatively short. So I cannot, on the basis of that, recognise -- reconcile that with the statement that you just put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Broeders. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Mr. Broeders, as far as the Prosecution understands, is VGD30 did not dispute that he had a conversation, but it was only a dispute what he really said. Now, if we look again at P109.2, the excerpt of the relevant portion we are concerned with which forms part of the 25 minutes -- do you still have the copy?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Somewhere, no doubt. Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: If you look at that copy, from lines 4, when the relevant portion starts, to line 15, did you find any indication of interruption or that it had been stopped, tampered or over-recorded with?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: From lines 16 to 26, have you found there any interruptions?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And is there anything on it that would indicate to you that it is not VGD30 we are talking about on this recording?

utterances.speaker: TON BROEDERS
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: That the statements that Prosecution attributes to VGD30 in this excerpt sound to me as though they were coming from the same person, okay? So, in other words, that is what I can say and that is also, I think, what is -- can be said on the basis partly again of this linguistic and phonetic analysis. So in other words, I would not like to suggest that the utterances here are from different speakers. I would also point out that it would be somewhat unlikely, in view of the nature of the conversation, for there to be more speakers involved. It wouldn't make too much sense probably if, you know, this conversation took place between various people. This part, I mean. In other words, it sounds like a dialogue at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Broeders. No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir, for coming to give evidence and for the evidence which you have given. You're now free to leave. Mr. Domazet, that other document that you have given us, the English translation of the Official Gazette with Articles 153 and 154 of the relevant statute, that will be Exhibit D45.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may make an inquiry regarding that particular document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's my understanding that -- I guess what I'm just curious about is, is this still an issue, the law -- is it still an issue that I need to deal with in my closing submission? It was my impression that the recordings were admitted and that this will not be an issue, what the law in Yugoslavia is regarding the recording of conversations. If it is, I'd just like to know so I can address it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If I may say so, that's all you need to say, but the point was taken that they were in opposition to provisions of a statute. We asked him for the terms of the statute. We were shown an opinion which didn't refer to them, so we asked to have it completed. But the document has been -- I'm sorry, the tape has been admitted notwithstanding these provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's just to complete the record on it. That's why I didn't bother to ask you whether you objected to it because it was a matter I thought we'd made clear before. We wanted to have it complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm just being cautious, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's all right. Yes, Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one small problem we have been made aware of. P113 is actually mentioning the name of the protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will place it under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And we would make then a redacted public version as P113.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: As soon as you bring it along, yes, it will be marked, because we want to be able to refer to the contents in any judgement we give.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And another information, the slides of this morning, one colour copy has been done and copies will be reproduced and delivered to the Chamber Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is it of each stage that he showed us these arrows?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Because it will be very difficult to read the transcript unless we have something like this, and it is in the same order that he dealt with. You may have to provide an operator as well, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I'm just advised we could also get the whole PowerPoint presentation, how it is presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I heard it all. It came through the sound system. But it would be very good if it could be checked that it's in the right order so that if we are reading his evidence, we will be able to follow it on these colour prints in the correct order. But thank you very much for that. Is there anything else we can deal with at this stage? We will be, I understand, in Courtroom II, back in the shoebox, next week. Now, how much work do you think we've got for next week, Mr. Groome? They are all your witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, recalling your admonition regarding the psychiatrist, I would hope to think that we would finish Monday, but especially in light of the other two fact witnesses I expect to be extremely brief, I hope to finish Monday.
